export default JSON.parse("{\"schema\":\"ai-brain-reference-analysis/1.0\",\"domain\":\"game-design\",\"capabilities\":[\"interactive-fiction\",\"command-routing\",\"state-machines\",\"combat\",\"inventory\",\"npc\",\"quest\",\"save-state\"],\"provenance\":{\"sourceType\":\"provided-reference-archives\",\"method\":\"file-structure and README capability extraction; third-party source code not redistributed\"},\"records\":[{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-001\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":1,\".sln\":1,\".h\":49,\".cpp\":9,\".vcxproj\":1,\".filters\":1,\".json\":1,\".md\":1,\".psd\":2},\"features\":[\"npc\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"

\\n

Octo-Spork

\\n \\n \\n \\n

\\n\\n### About\\n\\nOcto-Spork is a text-based adventure game I created for my assignment at University (Level 5). The story is that you are trapped inside an unknown building with three spirits blocking the path. You must search around the building to find a way to get out.\\n\\n### Code Explanation\\n\\nOcto-Spork is coded in C++ and meant to be run inside a console. The game, it's rooms and it's items are all loaded from \\\"Octo-Spork/Octo-Spork/resources/game.json\\\". [RapidJSON](https://rapidjson.org/) is being used to parse the json and extract the data into memory for being used. [OctoSpork.cpp](https://github.com/JoshLmao/Octo-Spork/blob/master/Octo-Spork/Octo-Spork/OctoSpork.cpp) also contains specific code for triggering the specific ending. However, you can change the game.json file to have extra or less rooms/items/npc's\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-002\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":5,\".yml\":2,\".md\":1,\".txt\":3,\".png\":1,\".gif\":1,\".cpp\":2,\".h\":1},\"features\":[\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# Adrift - a text adventure game\\n\\nA little game I wrote during my first year of coding. \\nA good way to learn git and C++.\\n\\n### How to run the game:\\nPull and run the 2.4MB Docker image: \\n`docker run -it --rm ghcr.io/mitchfen/adrift:latest`\\n\\n### Gameplay\\n\\n![adrift gif](./screenshots/adrift_gif.gif)\\n\\n\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-003\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":3,\".yml\":1,\".md\":2,\".gif\":1,\".clj\":12,\".js\":11,\".cljc\":18,\".cljs\":5},\"features\":[\"quest\",\"room\",\"map\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# advenjure [![Build Status](https://secure.travis-ci.org/facundoolano/advenjure.png)](http://travis-ci.org/facundoolano/advenjure)\\n\\n![Example game](example.gif)\\n\\nAdvenjure is a text adventure (or interactive fiction) game engine. I wrote it as an excuse to learn Clojure.\\nSome of its distinctive features are:\\n\\n * Target the terminal and the browser with the same codebase.\\n * Unix-like prompt with smart tab completion and command history\\n * Customizable verbs and plugins.\\n * LucasArts inspired dialog trees.\\n\\n## Example game\\n\\nYou can see the code for a working example in the [advenjure-example](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example) repository and play it online [here](https://facundoolano.github.io/advenjure).\\n\\nFor a fully fledged game see [House Taken Over](https://github.com/facundoolano/house-taken-over).\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\nAdd the following to your project map as a dependency:\\n\\n```clojure\\n[advenjure \\\"0.9.0\\\"]\\n```\\n\\n## Basic Usage\\n\\n### Creating items\\n\\nText adventures consist mainly of moving around rooms and interacting with items\\nthrough verb commands such as GO, LOOK, TAKE, etc.\\n\\nItems are represented by maps in advenjure. the `advenjure.items/make`\\nfunction takes a name, a description and a set of key-value pairs to customize behavior.\\nFor example:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.items :as items])\\n\\n(def magazine (items/make \\\"magazine\\\"\\n \\\"The cover read 'Sports Almanac 1950-2000'\\\"\\n :take true\\n :read \\\"Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0? Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0!?\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nThat will define a magazine item that can be taken (put in the player's inventory)\\nand can be read (which differs from looking at it).\\n\\nYou can provide a vector of names so the player can refer to it by one of its synonyms;\\nthe first name in the vector will be considered its canonical name:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def magazine (items/make [\\\"magazine\\\" \\\"sports magazine\\\" \\\"newspaper\\\"]\\n \\\"The cover read 'Sports Almanac 1950-2000'\\\"\\n :take true\\n :read \\\"Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0? Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0!?\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nLike `:take` and `:read` there are keywords for the other actions\\n(`:look-at`, `:open`, `:close`, `:unlock`, etc.).\\n\\nA special kind of items are those that can contain other items:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def magazine (items/make \\\"bag\\\" :items #{magazine} :closed true))\\n```\\n\\nThe bag contains the magazine, but since it's `:closed` the player needs to open it\\nbefore being able to look inside it and take its contents. Note that marking an\\nobject as `:closed` also implies that OPEN and CLOSE verbs can be applied to it\\n(i.e. it means `:open true, :close true`).\\n\\n### Creating rooms\\n\\nOnce you've created a bunch of items, you'll need to put them in a room (if not directly\\ninto the player's inventory). Rooms are also maps and also have an\\n`advenjure.rooms/make` function to build them:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.rooms :as rooms])\\n\\n(def bedroom (rooms/make \\\"Bedroom\\\"\\n \\\"A smelling bedroom.\\\"\\n :initial-description \\\"I woke up in a smelling little bedroom, without windows.\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nNote that rooms can have only one name. `:initial-description` is an optional attribute\\nto define how the player will describe a room the first time he visits it,\\nusually with a more verbose description. If `:initial-description` is not defined,\\nand whenever the LOOK AROUND command is entered, the regular description will be used.\\n\\nTo add items to a room use `advenjure.rooms/add-item`:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def bedroom (-> (rooms/make \\\"Bedroom\\\"\\n \\\"A smelling bedroom.\\\"\\n :initial-description \\\"I woke up in a smelling little bedroom, without windows.\\\")\\n (rooms/add-item (items/make \\\"bed\\\" \\\"It was the bed I slept in.\\\"))\\n (rooms/add-item magazine \\\"On the floor was a sports magazine.\\\")))\\n```\\n\\nThe second parameter is an optional room-specific description of the item. It will be used\\nto mention the item while describing the room (as opposed of the default `a is here.`).\\n\\n### Building a room map\\n\\nOnce you have some rooms, you need to connect them to build a room map, which is\\nnothing but a plain clojure hash map. First map the room to some id keyword,\\nthen connect the rooms using the `advenjure.rooms/connect` function:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def room-map (-> {:bedroom bedroom\\n :living living\\n :outside outside}\\n (rooms/connect :bedroom :north :living)\\n (rooms/connect :living :east :outside)))\\n```\\n\\nAn alternative function, `advenjure.rooms/one-way-connect`, allows connecting the\\nrooms just in one direction.\\n\\n### Building and running a game\\n\\nThe next building block is the game map itself, which contains the room map,\\nthe player's inventory and a pointer to the current room. `advenjure.game/make`\\nhelps to build it:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.game :as game])\\n\\n(game/make room-map :bedroom)\\n```\\n\\nThe room keyword defines what room the player will be in when the game starts.\\nIf you want to start off the game with some items in the player's inventory,\\njust pass them in a set as the third argument.\\n\\nLastly, the `advenjure.game/run` takes a game state map, a boolean function\\nto tell if the game has finished and an optional string to print before it starts.\\nPutting it all together in a `-main` function:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(defn -main\\n \\\"Build and run the game.\\\"\\n [& args]\\n (let [game-state (game/make room-map :bedroom)\\n finished? #(= (:current-room %) :outside)]\\n (game/run game-state finished? :start-message \\\"Welcome to the advenjure!\\\")))\\n```\\n\\nThe game flows by taking the initial game state map, prompting the user for a command,\\napplying the command to produce a new game state and repeat the process until the\\n`finished?` condition is met, which, in the example above means entering the\\n`:outside` room.\\n\\n## Advanced Usage\\n\\nThere is a number of advanced features available in the engine:\\n\\n * Overriding messages: use custom messages for a given action on a room or item.\\n * Pre conditions: function hook to define whether an action can be performed.\\n * Post conditions: function hook to customize how the game state is modified after an action is performed.\\n * Dialogs: interactive dialogs with 'character' items, in the style of the LucasArts graphic adventures.\\n * Text customization and internationalization.\\n * Custom verbs/commands.\\n * Plugin hooks to customize behavior without modifying the library.\\n\\nI'm waiting for the APIs to stabilize (and get a lot of free time) before fully documenting all those features,\\nbut I'd be happy to write something up if you need help with something specific, just file an issue!\\n\\n## Run on the browser\\n\\nThe codebase is prepared to run both in the terminal with Clojure and the browser with ClojureScript.\\nAn example configuration, using lein-cljsbuild would be:\\n\\n```clojure\\n:cljsbuild\\n {:builds\\n {:main {:source-paths [\\\"src\\\"]\\n :compiler {:output-to \\\"main.js\\\"\\n :main example.core\\n :optimizations :simple\\n :pretty-print false\\n :optimize-constants true\\n :static-fns true}}}\\n```\\n\\nThen the command `lein cljsbuild once` will output a `main.js` file that can be included in any web page to run the game.\\nThe HTML should have a `#terminal` div and include the [jQuery Terminal CSS](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example/blob/master/resources/jquery.terminal-0.11.7.css) to properly render the terminal.\\n\\nThe current limitations of the ClojureScript version of the library are:\\n* No internationalization support (since clojure-gettext does not support ClojureScript).\\n* Can use up to `:simple` optimizations (not `:advanced`), since [ClojureScript self-hosting](https://github.com/clojure/clojurescript/wiki/Optional-Self-hosting) is required for some of the advanced features.\\n\\nSee the [advenjure-example](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example) for a game that targets both the terminal and the browser.\\n\\n## Roadmap\\n\\n[Check the milestones](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure/milestones).\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-004\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".class\":7,\".ctxt\":5,\".java\":5,\"\":1,\".md\":1,\".txt\":1,\".bluej\":1,\".png\":1},\"features\":[\"room\",\"class\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# Adventure Game\\n\\nText based adventure game where, given a map, we were supposed to design a school building wherein the player is supposed to enter a building, find and retrieve a laptop, and exit the building to win. \\n\\nThere are several other objects to collect in the game including a flashlight, candy bar, and more. \\n\\n![Alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zimmertr/Adventure-Game/master/screenshot.png \\\"AG Screenshot\\\")\\n\\n## Winning and Losing\\n\\n**Steps to Win:**\\n\\n1) Move North \\n2) Move West \\n3) Pickup \\n4) Move Up \\n5) Light On \\n6) Move North \\n7) Pickup \\n8) Move South \\n9) Move Down \\n10) Move East \\n11) Move South \\n\\n\\n**Ways to Lose:**\\n\\n1) Break flashlight before collecting laptop - can't collect laptop without it \\n2) Break flashlight while in dark room - die of horror \\n3) Break the laptop any time - the object of the game is to collect the flashlight! \\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-005\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":2,\".txt\":3,\".java\":6},\"features\":[\"room\",\"item\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"Adventure, by Charlie Minges\\n\\n1: Introduction\\n2: Interacting with world\\n3: Goals\\n4: Text file format\\n\\n\\n1: Introduction\\n\\nWelcome to Adventure. In the coming hours, you will embark on a mysterious journey to escape the mysterious\\nlandscape that you have inexplicably woken up in. The best tool you have with you is the power of exploration.\\nIn order to ultimately escape, you will have to explore your surroundings, encountering a variety of items along\\nthe way. \\n\\n2: Interacting with the world\\n\\nNOTE: Commands are NOT case sensitive.\\n\\nLOOK\\nThere are many ways you can interact with the world around you. One of the first things you may want to do is \\nget a better idea of what is around you. To do this, you can use the look command. This will return a description\\nof the room you are in, as well as the possible directions you can move, and any items in the room at the time.\\nTo execute this command, simply type \\\"look\\\" into the console when given the opportunity.\\n\\nLOOK @ OBJECT\\nYou can also look at objects, along with rooms. To look at an object, type \\\"look\\\" followed by the name of the \\nobject you want to look at. It is IMPORTANT TO NOTE that you can only look at objects in your inventory. When \\nthis command is executed, you will be given the name of the object, as well as a short description for it. \\n\\nMOVE\\nThe next thing you will have to do to escape is move. Moving is quite simple. You must be aware that you are \\nallowed to move in the direction you desire from the room you are currently in. This information can be found \\nby looking at the room (SEE LOOK). To move, you either type \\\"move\\\" or \\\"go\\\" into the command line, followed by\\nthe desired direction (in terms of north, south, east, west). You can also just type in the direction you wish \\nto go. If you have moved successfully, a description of the new room you are in will be printed out to the \\nconsole.\\n\\nTAKE\\nItems are an important aspect of Adventure. One way you can interact with them is by taking them. If you are in \\na room that has an item, you can enter \\\"take\\\", or \\\"get\\\", followed by the item name, to add that item to your\\ninventory. This will subsequently remove the object from the rooms inventory.\\n\\nDROP\\nAlong with taking items, you can also drop them. To drop an item from your inventory, simply type in the command\\n\\\"drop\\\", followed by the name of the item you wish to drop. This will add the item to the rooms inventory, and remove\\nit from your own.\\n\\nOTHER\\nThe last two commands available to you, the player, are \\\"inventory\\\" and \\\"score\\\". Inventory will return the names \\nof all the items in your inventory, or tell you if it is empty. Score will return a number representing the score\\nyou have accumulated while playing. They are both accessed by typing in either \\\"inventory\\\" or \\\"score\\\", depending \\non which you want.\\n\\n3: Goals and Scoring\\n\\nThere are a variety of goals that the player should reach throughout the game before being able to escape. A goal \\nwill consist of either taking/dropping an item from/in a particular room, or visiting a particular room. When you \\ncomplete a goal, you get points. You need to complete all goals then visit a particular room in order to escape. The\\ngoal you need to meet for points is 500. Once you have 500 points, you will be directed to a particular particular\\nroom to complete your escape.\\n\\n4: Text file format\\n\\nText files are used to create the rooms and items, as well as guidelines for scoring. Due to this, they need to be\\nset up in a particular way. It is important to note that, whenever using room names, they must match exactly, including\\ncapitalization.\\n\\nROOMS\\nOne room object will read in three different pieces of information: name, neighbors, and description. In the text file,\\nthe information should be organized as follows...\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tname\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tnorth(room name), south(room name), east(room name), west(room name)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tdescription (can extend for multiple lines)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tEND\\nYou must add END, in all caps, at the end of one rooms description, in order for the program to make the distinction \\nthat it is going to make a new room. For the neighbors, put the names of the rooms to the north, south, east, and west\\n(must be done in order shown in example). If there are no neighbors to one direction, use -. You must also include END\\nfor the last rooms text description.\\n\\nITEMS\\nItems are handled in a similar fashion to rooms. They include information regarding name, starting location, and a short\\ndescription. The information should be set up as follows\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tname\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tstarting location (room name)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tdescription (can extend for multiple lines)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tEND\\nSimilar to rooms, END must be included at the end, so the program can make the distinction between two objects. You must\\nalso include END after the last items text description.\\n\\nSCORING\\nScoring information includes the type of action (take, drop, visit), the object involved (if there is one), the room it\\nmust take place in, and the points awarded. The information should be set up as follows\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\taction, item, room, points\\nIf the action does not involve an item, put a - where an item name would otherwise go. No single segment of information \\nfor one Score object should extend beyond one line.\\n\\n\\nThank you for reading me! Now go enjoy the game, and email me at charles.minges@hws.edu if you have any more questions.\",\"licenseIndicators\":[]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-006\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":3,\".yml\":1,\".in\":1,\".md\":1,\".py\":5,\".rst\":9,\".ini\":1},\"features\":[\"command\",\"room\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# adventurelib\\n\\n[![Build](https://travis-ci.org/lordmauve/adventurelib.svg?branch=master)\\n](https://travis-ci.org/lordmauve/adventurelib)\\n[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/adventurelib/badge/?version=latest)](https://adventurelib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)\\n\\n`adventurelib` provides basic functionality for writing text-based adventure\\ngames, with the aim of making it easy enough for young teenagers to do.\\n\\nThe foundation of adventurelib is the ability to define functions that are\\ncalled in response to commands. For example, you could write a function to\\nbe called when the user types commands like \\\"take hat\\\":\\n\\n @when('take THING')\\n def take(thing):\\n print(f'You take the {thing}.')\\n inventory.append(thing)\\n\\nIt also includes the foundations needed to write games involving rooms, items,\\ncharacters and more... but users will have to implement these features for\\nthemselves as they explore Python programming concepts.\\n\\n## Installing\\n\\n`adventurelib.py` is a single file that can be copied into your project. You\\ncan also install it with pip:\\n\\n pip install adventurelib\\n\\n\\n## Documentation\\n\\n[Comprehensive documentation is on Read The Docs.](http://adventurelib.readthedocs.io/)\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-007\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".yml\":2,\"\":7,\".xml\":1,\".lock\":1,\".ide\":1,\".ide-shm\":1,\".ide-wal\":1,\".config\":1,\".json\":9,\".csproj\":6,\".cs\":342,\".txt\":1,\".ico\":1,\".js\":1,\".sln\":1,\".md\":1},\"features\":[\"combat\",\"quest\",\"command\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"save\",\"map\",\"movement\",\"random\",\"event\",\"character\",\"class\",\"skill\",\"item\",\"world\",\"layer\",\"effect\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# ArchaicQuest II - MUD codebase written in C#\\n![alt ArchaicQuest II](https://i.imgur.com/LUv3vGm.png)\\n\\n## A MUD codebase to create a multiplayer text based RPG, also known a Multi User Dungeon (MUD)\\n\\nGoal of ArchaicQuest II is to make a MUD that feels nostalgic and compelling to play as well as providing a MUD codebase that makes building and managing your own game simple and fun especially for non coders with the help of the admin tool.\\n\\n[play.archaicquest.com](https://play.archaicquest.com) is the flagship MUD built with ArchaicQuest II.\\n\\n## Current Features\\n- Currently 54 commands, commands can also be abbreviated \ud83d\udd20\\n- Cardinal and Ordinal Movement directions including up and down \ud83e\uddb6\\n- Auto Attack combat rounds \u2694\\n- Skills & spells \ud83d\udcab\\n- 350+ socials \ud83d\ude03 \\n- Look, examine, smell, taste, and touch objects \ud83d\udc41\ud83d\udd0e\ud83d\udc43\ud83d\udc45\ud83e\udd0f\\n- Day and Night cycles \ud83c\udf1e\ud83c\udf1b\\n- Communication among players publicly and privately \ud83d\udcac\\n- NPCs can follow waypoints and execute commands \ud83c\udfad\\n- Ability to add simple or complex quests with Lua Scripting \u2049\\n- Event scripts for NPCs/Rooms for your scripting needs \ud83d\udcdc\\n- Room and NPC emotes \ud83d\udc83\\n\\n## About the Projects\\n\\nArchaicQuest II comprises of [3 projects](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest) that are required together.\\n\\n\\n| Project | Description |\\n| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II) | C# game engine, contains the web API for the admin tool and the SignalR hub for the web socket connects to the client. |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II - Admin tool](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II-Web-Admin) | Angular 8+ web admin, allows creation and management of your MUD world. |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II - Game Client](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II-Web-Client) | Angular 8+ web client for connecting to the game and playing with others. |\\n\\n## ArchaicQuest II\\n\\nThe C# project is .NET Core 3.1 and uses [LiteDb](https://www.litedb.org/) which is an embedded NoSQL database. Within Startup.cs it will seed the database on first run with the necessary defaults that are required. \\n\\n* Alignments\\n* AttackTypes\\n* Skills\\n* Races\\n* Status\\n* Classes\\n* Config\\n\\nSome of the above can be edited in the admin tool, the rest if required to be changed needs to be done in code.\\n\\nThe last important step that isn't seeded yet is the very first room! For now before connecting to the game you will need to fire up the web admin tool and create an area and then create a room in said area. Then the web client will be able to connect correctly. \\n\\n### Running the project\\nUse `dotnet run --project ArchaicQuestII.API/ArchaicQuestII.API.csproj`.\\n\\nIf on unix you can use the make file in the project to run using `make run`. \\n\\nFor Windows using visual studio just hit the run button.\\n\\nThere's no output to say it's running but once you make a request it wakes up and responds.\\n\\n### Basic Structure overview\\n\\n- ArchaicQuestII.API\\n - Handles all the API endpoints and initialises everything in Startup.cs\\n- ArchaicQuestII.DataAccess\\n - Wrapper around LiteDB. To add new collections you need to modify Collections enum and the GetCollectionName switch\\n- ArchaicQuestII.GameLogic\\n - All game logic here plus the SignalR and Telnet logic. Best place to start is Commands.cs to see what commands exists and how to add more.\\n \\n### Adding Commands / Features\\n\\nView the existing structure in Commands.cs there may be an interface where you can add your new command. If not follow the existing structure to add a new interface and class and make sure to update the tests once you add the new interface to Commands.cs \\n\\nTo add new skills and spells use the web admin tool, skills and spells can be scripted with Lua for custom formulas and effects.\\n\\nMajority of features added have been built with the admin tool in mind so most content can be added or modified without coding or making a deployment\\n\\n### Telnet Support\\nTraditionally MUDs use telnet as the way to communicate but with ArchaicQuest II it's web only, the browser can offer a richer, consistent, and streamlined interface for all players without having them to download a client. \\n\\n### Want to get involved?\\nIf you're a coder, writer, MUD player, or someone who wants to help up then get in touch and say 'Hello' on the discord server: [https://discordapp.com/invite/nuf7FVq](https://discordapp.com/invite/nuf7FVq)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Admin Tool\\nView the [ArchaicQuest II - Game Client](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II-Web-Client) to find out more.\\n\\n![alt ArchaicQuestII Web Admin](https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/660365544377155604/764419914970300456/web_client.PNG)\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-008\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":7,\".cs\":323,\".csproj\":4,\".config\":18,\".sln\":1,\".css\":5,\".cshtml\":38,\".tsx\":5,\".json\":6,\".scss\":93,\".html\":4,\".js\":27,\".asax\":2,\".ico\":2,\".txt\":5,\".jpg\":11,\".db\":1,\".map\":2,\".md\":4,\".eot\":3,\".svg\":3,\".ttf\":3,\".woff\":3,\".yml\":1,\".png\":1,\".defaults\":1,\".backup\":1,\".xml\":1},\"features\":[\"quest\",\"command\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"save\",\"map\",\"movement\",\"event\",\"character\",\"class\",\"skill\",\"item\",\"world\",\"layer\",\"effect\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# [RPG Awesome](http://nagoshiashumari.github.io/Rpg-Awesome/)\\n### A fantasy themed font and CSS toolkit.\\n\\nRPG Awesome is a suite of 495 pictographic, rpg and fantasy themes icons for easy scalable vector graphics on websites, created and maintained by [Daniela Howe](https://github.com/nagoshiashumari) and [Ivan Montiel](http://github.com/idmontie).\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\n### Bower\\n\\n```\\nbower install rpg-awesome\\n```\\n\\n### NPM\\n\\n```\\nnpm add --save rpg-awesome\\n```\\n\\n### Meteor\\n\\n```\\nmeteor add rpg-awesome\\n```\\n\\n## Developing\\n\\nThis project uses NPM and Grunt to compile SCSS into CSS usable by browsers.\\nThe project also requires for you to have Ruby installed:\\n\\n```sh\\nnpm install\\ngem update --system && gem install scss-lint\\ngrunt\\n```\\n\\n## Generating and Adding New Icons\\n\\nWe have split up the generation process of the `/fonts` directory to\\n[this repo](https://github.com/nagoshiashumari/rpg-awesome-raw).\\n\\nAny new icons will need to be added to that repo first. Bilderbeek [1], Rafayel Gardishyan [2], Rob Krueger [2], \\n Rijk van Putten, Joshua van Waardenberg [2]\\n\\n * [1] Corresponding author\\n * [2] Contributed to the work equally, sorted alphabetically on last name \\n\\n## Abstract\\n\\nCity of Thieves is a text adventure in the form of a book.\\nTo beat it, a player has to make the right choices, in a stochastic environment.\\nThe optimal strategy to beat this game is unknown.\\nHere we show the optimal strategy to beat this game.\\n[prime result here].\\n\\n## Introduction\\n\\nIn the 1980's, before the era of computing, adventure books\\nallowed the reader to partake a fictional adventure.\\nAdventure books consisted of hundreds of short chapters in\\na random order. The reader starts at chapter 1 and is asked\\nto do one of multiple actions. Each action takes the player\\nto a next chapter. The player ultimately completes the game\\nor dies.\\n\\n![](Ff5puffin.jpg)\\n\\n> Cover of the first edition of 'City of Thieves'\\n\\nCity of Thieves is a an adventure book written by Ian Livingstone in 1984.\\nThe player should venture to the castle of the protagonist,\\nafter having visited a certain person in a medieval city,\\nthe titular 'City of Thieves'. \\n\\nA character has three statistics: health, skill and luck. \\nMore health allows a player to take more damage,\\nfor example, taking hits in combat.\\nMore skill allows a player to be better in combat,\\nas well as succeed in certain situations, \\nfor example, [example].\\nMore luck allows a player in a situation that requires luck,\\nfor example, when an arrow trap springs, luck may let the player \\navoid the (lethal!) arrow.\\n\\nThese three statistics can be modified within the game.\\nHealth can be increased by certain items, such as food. \\nHealth decreases when taking damage, which is usually in combat,\\nbut can also stem from other physical injuries, such as falling down a wall.\\nSkill can be increased by certain items, such as a better sword.\\nSkill can be decreased by other such items, such as cursed gloves that\\ndecrease the dexterity of the wearer.\\nLuck can be increased by certain events or items, \\nsuch as hearing a blessed song.\\nLuck decreases mostly by using it (see below) or by certain events, such as \\nkilling one of the key characters.\\n\\nThe game starts with a character generation session, \\nsimilar to most RPGs.\\nFor one or more times, 4 dice are rolled.\\nIn a pre-defined order, the dice values determine the\\nplayer's characteristics.\\nA player's skill equals the first dice roll value plus three (this \\ndeviates from the game, see 'Discussion'), the condition is the sum of two dice rolls,\\nwhere luck is the last dice roll value plus six.\\nThe player may roll as often as possible, allowing to get the best values,\\nbut this is quite dull.\\nAccording to Livingstone, the adventure is constructed in such\\na way, that these dice rolls are of less importance. It is unknown,\\nhowever, if the game can be completed with the worst dice rolls.\\n\\nAfter the character generation session, a player may pick\\none of three potions, for either of the three statistics.\\nWhere the health and skill potion refresh their respective value\\nto the initial value, a luck potion does so, as well as add one additional \\npoint. It is an open question, which potion is best to pick\\n\\nAt the start of the game, the player starts with [items] and [number] \\ngold coins. These items may be lost or sold. \\nThe gold coins are used as a currency, to buy items or other situations,\\nsuch as bribing a guard.\\n\\nWithin the actual game, there are multiple kinds of chapters.\\nThe most common type of chapter is to pick one of multiple\\nactions. Sometimes some actions can only be picked after having\\nacquired a certain item [example here]. The other types of chapters\\nare fighting chapters, logical chapters, luck chapters and skill chapters.\\n\\nIn a fighting chapter, the player fights one, two or three opponents.\\nAll opponents have a know value for their health and skill, that\\nare similar to the player. The goal of the player, is to \\nsucceed in combat, by bringing down the health of opponents to zero.\\nLikewise, when an opponent hits the player, its health goes down,\\nwhere a health of zero ends the game. \\nA player can use luck to increase the damage dealt to the enemy,\\nor to decrease the damage dealth by that enemy. Using luck decreases its\\nvalue, decreasing the change of a positive event in successive usages. \\n\\nA logical chapter is simply a conditional statement\\nregarding the possession of an item. For example, when the\\nplayer leaves the city, he/she needs to possess some key items,\\nelse the game is over.\\n\\nLuck and skill chapters are similar: a player needs to roll the dice\\nto test his/her skill or luck, after which a different chapter follows\\ndepending the success of this. An example of a skill chapter is [example].\\nAn example of a luck chapter is [example]. The only additional difference\\nis that using luck decrease that statistic.\\n\\nThe adventure starts at the gates of the city, the first city\\nstreets, a bridge at which a vital character lives, some more city streets,\\nafter which the city is left. If the player has acquired some esstial items,\\nthe adventure goes through a forest, followed by the keep of the protagonist.\\nThe story always go forwards, that is each location can only be visited once,\\nas the player cannot venture back.\\nThere is only location (the keep's 2nd and 3rd [check] floor) in which\\na location can be visited multiple times, but doing so is either\\nneutral or detrimental.\\n\\nBecause the player cannot go back and the player needs to acquire some\\nessential items, some decisions cause the player to lose the game due to\\nthis. For example, at the first junction after crossing the bridge,\\nthe player must go towards the [name] street to acquire such a key item,\\nafter which the game takes the player back to follow the other street \\nafterwards. Therefore, reaching the latter location on itself is uninformative:\\nonly with the key item acquired the player has a change of winning the game.\\nThe state transition, however, is informative: going from that \\njunction directly to the final destination (without getting the\\nkey item) is a sure fail.\\n\\nUpon passing the city gate, there is junction, in which the player\\nhas to choose one of three streets. None of these streets contain an\\nessential item and all lead to the same bridge. Yet, these three routes\\nvary in the items a player can find as well as the amount of danger.\\nIt is unknown which of these three streets results in the\\nhighest chance of success.\\n\\nThis research answers all the questions a player of 'City of Thieves'\\nmay have, solving one more puzzle that has plagued humanity for decades.\\n\\n## Hypotheses\\n\\n * H_0: the dice rolls at the start of the game do not influence the\\n chance of winning the game, when the game is played optimally\\n * H_1: the potion picked at the start of the game do not influence the\\n chance of winning the game, when the game is played optimally\\n * H_2: it does not matter which of the three streets is picked at the initial\\n junction for the chance of winning the game, when the game is played optimally\\n\\n## Methods\\n\\nTo allow the game to be solved by a computer, it has been converted\\nto a computer game. \\n\\nWe used [a] technique to answer the hypotheses.\\n\\nWe picked this technique, because [...]\\n\\nAssigning pay-off values to certain location is expected to fail,\\nas only a location is uninformative. For example, one can reach a certain\\nlocation by taking a short-cut, yet without acquiring an essential item. \\n\\nAssigning pay-off values to certain choices is expected to be more \\nviable, as this will allow an algorithm to take a detour to obtain\\na vital item.\\n\\nTo answer H_0 and H_1, we measure the change to win the game, when played\\noptimally, for the different initial statistics and potion. If all chances\\nare all equal, H_0 and H_1 is accepted. If chances differ between the\\ndifferent statistics, H0 is rejected. If chances are all identical, yet\\ndiffer per initial potion, H_1 is rejected.\\n\\nTo answer H_2, we measure the payoff the optimal stategy assigns to\\neither of the three streets. If these payoffs are equal, H_2 is accepted,\\nelse H2 is rejected.\\n\\n### Rob's idea, Q-Learning:\\n\\nQ-learning works with rewards, so you can get a reward for acquiring a good \\nitem or for completing the game. For every state, the chapter and all\\nthe items in this case, it gives a certain value to every possible action. \\nIt isn't 'short-sighted', so it won't do a certain action if that action gives \\nhim a reward but there aren't any good moves afterwards. \\n![](Q-Learning_1.jpg)\\n\\n[RJCB: I enjoy this figure! Describe what is that\\nmaxQ thingie :+1:]\\n\\nThe rewards are values between -1 and 1 [RJCB: For figure 1, using values\\nfor zero (always die) to 1.0 (win the game) would probably be more\\nnatural. Feel free to ignore this though :+1:]. \\nThe tricky part is assigning the rewards [RJCB: the rewards at the nodes, and/or at the edges?]. \\nWhat do you define as a good move? \\nI think the reward should be a small negative reward if the action didn't \\nresult in a condition loss, but also not resulted in acquiring a good item. \\nThis will prevent it for walking in a loop. If a action resulted in a condition \\nloss, then it should get a slightly bigger negative reward. For losing the game, \\nthe reward is obviously -1. For winning the game, the reward is 1. Acquiring a \\nvital item results in a reward of 0.5-0.6. Acquiring a regular item results in a\\nsmall reward of 0.2 [RJCB: again, not all items are positive to have!].\\n\\n[RJCB: make the link to the results. Does this method help accept/reject all three\\nhypotheses?]\\n\\n### Rafayel's idea: Multi-run\\n\\n[RJCB: go ahead and remove all comments :+1:]\\n\\nThe game has a class `ai.cpp` which generates a `.dot` file at startup. This contains all the nodes and the connections between them. Also it contains all the vital items.\\nIt would be logical to use this file instead of the whole game to make the process simpler.\\n\\nThe process begins with an algorithm which runs trough the game many times and gives each node a score. At startup all nodes have a score of `1` which changes every time the bot reaches the end (`game win` or `game over`). This happens with the following rules:\\n1. The bot, when it gets started travels downwards the graph by choosing the node with the highest score. If the scores are equal one of the nodes is being chosen randomly.\\n2. Please see [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/microsoft/debug-gym/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) for recent updates.\\n\\n## 1. Installation\\n\\nIt's recommended to create and activate a conda or virtual environment. `debug-gym` requires `Python>=3.12`:\\n\\n conda create -n debug-gym python=3.12\\n conda activate debug-gym\\n\\nThen, install `debug-gym` directly from PyPI:\\n\\n pip install debug-gym\\n\\nAlternatively, clone the repository and install locally:\\n\\n git clone https://github.com/microsoft/debug-gym\\n cd debug-gym\\n pip install -e .\\n\\nTo install development dependencies, run:\\n\\n pip install -e '.[dev]'\\n\\n\\n**Set your API information in llm.yaml**\\n\\nFirst, create an LLM config template by running `python -m debug_gym.llms.configure`:\\n\\n python -m debug_gym.llms.configure\\n\\n> [!TIP]\\n> Run `python -m debug_gym.llms.configure --help` for more options. By default, the template is created at `$HOME/.config/debug_gym/llm.yaml`, but you can specify any directory.\\n\\nThen, edit this file with your endpoint and credentials. You can choose one of these authentication methods:\\n- For authenticating with an API key, provide `api_key`.\\n- For `az login` or Managed Identity authentication on Azure, remove `api_key` and include `scope` instead.\\n\\n> [!WARNING]\\n> When using open-sourced LLMs, e.g., via vLLM, you need to correctly setup `HF_TOKEN` required by the tokenizer. You can also provide `tokenizer_kwargs` in your `llm.yaml` entry (for example `trust_remote_code: true`) to control how the Hugging Face tokenizer is instantiated.\\n\\nBy default, `debug-gym` looks for the LLM config file at `$HOME/.config/debug_gym/llm.yaml`. You can change this behavior by exporting the environment variable `LLM_CONFIG_FILE_PATH` or by setting `llm_config_file_path` in your script config file (see [Running Baselines](#3-running-baselines)).\\n\\n**Overriding LLM parameters in experiment configs**\\n\\nYou can override LLM generation parameters like `temperature` and `max_tokens` directly in your experiment config file under the `llm:` section. These values take precedence over the defaults in `llm.yaml`:\\n\\n```yaml\\nllm:\\n name: gpt-4o\\n temperature: 0.7 # optional, overrides llm.yaml default\\n max_tokens: 4096 # optional, overrides llm.yaml default\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. System Design\\n\\nThe structure of `debug-gym` is as below:\\n```bash\\ndebug_gym\\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 gym\\n\u2502 \u251c\u2500\u2500 envs\\n\u2502 \u251c\u2500\u2500 terminals\\n\u2502 \u2514\u2500\u2500 tools\\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 agents\\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 llms\\n```\\n\\n`debug_gym.gym` is a simulation environment. Given a code repository, an agent can iteratively interact with a set of tools, such as `pdb`, that are designed for investigate the code. Once gathered enough information, the agent can propose a patch that edits certain lines of the code. The terminal will subsequently execute the new code against a set of test cases.\\n\\n`debug_gym.agents` are LLM-based debugging agents that use `debug_gym.gym` to interact with code repositories to seek necessary information and thus fix potential bugs. At an interaction step, the agent takes a text observation that describes the environment states and tool states as input, it is expected to generate a command, subsequently, the environment will provide a new text observation in response, describing the state change caused by that command.\\n\\n`debug_gym.llms` are the different LLM backends that can be used to instantiate agents. Currently, we support OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Hugging Face/vLLM deployments (via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint), and Anthropic. For Hugging Face models served through vLLM, the tokenizer's chat template is applied automatically to ensure token counting and truncation match the hosted model.\\n\\n> [!WARNING]\\n> `debug-gym` has limited support on non-Linux platforms. Interactive terminal sessions using PTY (pseudo-terminal) in Docker are not fully supported on macOS or Windows. As a result, the `pdb` tool (see [2.1. Environment and Tools](#21-environment-and-tools)) only works on Linux.\\n\\n---\\n\\n#### 2.1. Environment and Tools\\n\\nOur base environment, `RepoEnv`, is an interactive environment that follows the [Gymnasium](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Gymnasium) paradigm. Once the environment `env` is instantiated, one can use `env.reset()` to start an episode and receives initial informations. Then, one can interact with the environment using `env.step(action)`, where `action` specifies one of the available tools (see below), doing so will return subsequent informations (e.g, error message, debugger stdout, etc.)\\n\\nOne of the core designs of `debug-gym` is the notion of tools. Users can dynamically import tools, or develop customized tools and utilize them in the environment. Tools are modules that augment an agent's action space, observation space, or provide additonal functionalities to the agent. Below are the set of tools we have implemented so far.\\n\\n| Tool name | Description |\\n| :-: | :----- |\\n| `bash` | Run commands in a bash shell. You have access to common Linux and Python packages via pip. State is persistent across command calls within the same session. |\\n| `view` | It is used to change an agent's focus to a particular source code file. This is particularly useful when dealing with a repository with multiple files. |\\n| `eval` | It runs the current code repository using the provided entrypoint (e.g., pytest), and returns the terminal's output (e.g., error message). |\\n| `pdb` | Interactive debugger wrapping the [Python pdb tool](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pdb.html). In addition, users can choose to maintain a set of persistent breakpoints (as in some programming IDEs), which are not reset after every eval. With such feature, a new pdb debugging session is activated automatically, with all the breakpoints restored. Note such breakpoints can be cleared by pdb commands such as `cl`. |\\n| `grep` | Search for patterns in files within the repository. Supports both literal string matching and regular expressions. Can search in specific files, directories, or the entire repository. Useful for finding code patterns, function definitions, variable usage, or identifying files containing specific text. |\\n| `listdir` | List the file and folder contents of a directory within the working directory, up to a specified depth. Useful for exploring the repository structure. |\\n| `edit` | It can be used to edit a certain piece of code to fix the bug. The inputs of this tool call include the file path, the start and end line numbers, and the new code. |\\n| `submit` | Submit your changes once the task is complete. By default, it runs evaluation before terminating the session, but this can be disabled via `eval_on_submit: false`. |\\n| MCP tools | Dynamically register tools from external MCP servers. See [MCP Proxy Tool](debug_gym/gym/tools/MCP_README.md) for details. |\\n\\nUpon importing a tool, its action space and observation space will be automatically merged into `debug-gym`'s action space and observation space; its instruction will also be merged into the overall instruction provided to the agent (e.g., as system prompt).\\n\\n**Tool Dependencies:** Some tools require additional packages to be installed in the terminal environment. When a tool is added to the configuration, its required dependencies are automatically installed during terminal setup. For example, the `listdir` tool requires the `tree` package, which is automatically installed when the tool is used. This ensures that tools work out of the box without manual configuration.\\n\\n---\\n\\n#### 2.2. Agents\\n\\nWe provide the below LLM-based agents, they all have minimal design and serve the purpose of demonstrating the `debug-gym` APIs.\\n\\n| Agent name | Available Tools | Description |\\n| :-: | :-: | :----- |\\n| `froggy_agent` | `bash`, `view`, `edit`, `submit` (configurable) | Primary debugging agent. Adjust prompts and tool lists in YAML to customize workflows. |\\n| `solution_agent` | `pdb`, `eval` | An oracle agent that applies a gold patch (works with `swebench`, `swesmith`, and `r2egym` benchmarks). The agent checks that tests are failing before applying the patch, and passing after. It also checks that `pdb` tool can be used as expected (if available). |\\n\\n---\\n\\n#### 2.3. Benchmarks\\n\\nTo demonstrate how to integrate `debug-gym` with coding tasks and repositories, we provide example code importing widely used benchmarks, namely `aider`, `swebench`, `swesmith` and `r2egym`, and a small set of minimal buggy code snippets, namely `mini_nightmare`.\\n\\n| Benchmark name | Link |\\n| :-: | :----- |\\n| `aider` | [https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider](https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider) |\\n| `swebench`| [https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench](https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench) |\\n| `swesmith`| [https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-smith](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-smith) |\\n| `r2egym`| [https://github.com/R2E-Gym/R2E-Gym](https://github.com/R2E-Gym/R2E-Gym) |\\n| `mini_nightmare` | A set of 10 hand-crafted minimal buggy code snippet where edit-only agents have harder time to tackle. Read details [here](https://github.com/microsoft/debug-gym/blob/main/data/mini_nightmare/mini_nightmare.md). |\\n\\n> [!NOTE]\\n> Since debug-gym focuses on debugging tasks with the use of a debugger, we provide a customized version of `swebench`, called `swebench-debug`, where each problem's codebase already has the gold test patch applied. This allows us to better simulate real-world debugging scenarios where the buggy code is expected to have failing tests and we can set the debugger's entrypoint accordingly. To use `swebench-debug`, use `configs/swebench_debug.yaml` or set `dataset.type: swebench-debug` in your config file.\\n\\n---\\n\\n#### 2.4. Terminals\\n\\n`debug-gym` supports multiple terminal backends to accommodate different execution environments and deployment scenarios. Each terminal type provides a consistent interface while handling the underlying infrastructure differently.\\n\\n| Terminal Type | Description |\\n| :-: | :----- |\\n| `LocalTerminal` | Executes commands directly on the local machine using bash. Ideal for development and testing on local systems. |\\n| `DockerTerminal` | Executes commands inside Docker containers running on your machine. Provides isolated execution environments. (Recommended) |\\n| `KubernetesTerminal` | Executes commands in Kubernetes pods for scalable deployments. Provides isolated execution environments. Suitable when dealing with large benchmarks like `swebench`, `swesmith`, and `r2egym`. |\\n\\nAll terminals support:\\n- Specify custom working directories and session commands\\n- Environment variable configuration\\n- Command execution with timeout handling\\n- Output capturing and error reporting\\n- Automatic cleanup and resource management\\n- Retry mechanisms for transient errors\\n- Provide a way to create persistent interactive shell sessions using pseudo-terminals (PTY). Used internally by interactive debugging tools such as `pdb`.\\n> [!WARNING]\\n> Interactive shell sessions are not fully compatible with macOS due to their reliance on pty.\\n\\nTerminal selection is configured through the `terminal_config` in your script configuration file. The framework automatically handles terminal initialization, command execution, and cleanup based on the specified type.\\n\\n---\\n\\n#### 2.5. Timeouts\\n\\n`debug-gym` provides several timeout mechanisms to ensure agents don't hang indefinitely:\\n\\n| Timeout Type | Description | Default | Configuration |\\n| :-: | :----- | :-: | :----- |\\n| **Command Timeout** | Maximum time for a single command (e.g., `bash`, `eval`) to execute. Prevents blocking commands like `serve_forever()` or infinite loops from hanging the agent. | 300s (5 min) | `terminal.command_timeout` |\\n| **Run Timeout** | Maximum time for a single eval/ru\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-014\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":5,\".yml\":1,\".md\":1,\".png\":2,\".cfg\":1,\".desktop\":1,\".xml\":1,\".c\":84,\".h\":96,\".mk\":1},\"features\":[\"save\",\"map\",\"state\",\"random\",\"event\",\"item\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# DOOM-ASCII\\n\\n![LOGO](screenshots/logo.png)\\n\\n**Text-based DOOM in your terminal!**\\n\\nSource-port of [doomgeneric](https://github.com/ozkl/doomgeneric). The door ahead is shut, yet there must be way to open it.\\nThe question is, do you want to? Are you ready to face what might be waiting on the other side?\\n\\nHint: Picking up a sword and a shield will help.\\n\\n# Contents\\n**[Project Goals](#project-goals)**
\\n**[Building and Running](#building-and-running)**
\\n**[Screenshots](#screenshots)**

\\n\\n# Project Goals\\n\\n- Practice C++.\\n- Create a Text Adventure Game Engine in C++ using reusable design patterns.\\n- Implement a simple text adventure game using the engine called 'First Adventure'.\\n\\nThe aim of this project is to practice C++11, design patterns and do some basic game development. \\nAs this is an education exercise, some of the code is purposefully over engineered and the implemented story simple.\\n\\n# Building and Running\\n\\nBuilt and run on a Mac running macOS 10.13.2 (C++11).\\n\\nTo build and run you can either:\\n\\na. Checkout and import into XCode.\\n\\nb. Checkout and run CMake in the folder containing the CMakeLists.txt file to create a Makefile.\\nThen navigate to the Makefile and run Make to create an executable.\\n\\nFollow the ingame instructions to navigate through the game.\\n\\n# Screenshots\\n\\n### Your First Choice\\n\\n![Alt text](screenshots/FirstAdventure_FirstChoice.png?raw=true \\\"Your first choice\\\")\\n\\n### You need a key to unlock some doors!\\n\\n![Alt text](screenshots/FirstAdventure_UnlockingDoorsWithoutKey.png?raw=true \\\"You need a key to unlock some doors!\\\")\\n\\n### Good thing you can open chests and pick up items\\n\\n![Alt text](screenshots/FirstAdventure_PickingUpItems.png?raw=true \\\"Good thing you can open chests and pick up items\\\")\\n\\n### If you've found the right key you can unlock doors\\n\\n![Alt text](screenshots/FirstAdventure_UnlockingDoorsWithKey.png?raw=true \\\"Now you can unlock the doors\\\")\\n\\n### But do you really want to? Lucky we found that shield...\\n\\n![Alt text](screenshots/FirstAdventure_AttackingDragons.png?raw=true \\\"But do you really want to? Lucky we found that shield...\\\")\\n\\n\\n\\n# Learning C++\\n\\nIt's been really fun learning C++ over the past few weeks.\\n\\nMy favourite part has been the freedom and control it gives to developers when doing pretty much anything (see \\\"Instance Creation On Stack vs Heap\\\" for an example).\\n\\nI enjoy the challenge of understanding how the compiler works, how my code is executed by the Operating System, and how I can make it more efficient whilst keeping it easy to understand.\\n\\n### Why learn C++?\\n\\nMy day job focuses on building and designing high performant, scalable, fault tolerant, reusable systems in Java.\\n\\nThese systems are critical to the day-to-day running of the business.\\n\\nThrough C++ I've seen how much the Java Compiler hides from developers in terms of memory management, instance creation, and just about anything else.\\n\\nC++ has provided a better understanding on what happens behind the scenes when coding in Java and how my OS runs my applications.\\n\\n### Resources\\n\\n- Learn C++ for Game Development by Bruce Sutherland (ISBN-13: 978-1430264576)\\n- Game Programming Patterns by Robert Nystrom (ISBN: 0990582906)\\n\\n### Instance Creation On Stack vs Heap\\n\\nIt was interesting to understand the different ways C++ let's you create objects and manage their memory; a fundamental concept for an object oriented language.\\n\\nThis was something I did not think about when writing Java code.\\n\\n(Note: I'm assuming a basic understanding of memory management in Java / Operating Systems -e.g. what is the heap, stack, pass by reference, pass by value)\\n\\nIn Java you create an instance of a class as:\\n\\n
\\nMyClass myInstance = new MyClass();\\n
\\n\\n- What does this mean?\\n\\nJava is actually creating a reference that points to an instance (an area of memory) of MyClass on the heap.\\n\\nThis is why you can change the field values of an instance inside a method, even though Java is 'pass-by-value':\\nhttps://www.journaldev.com/4098/java-heap-space-vs-stack-memory\\n\\nIn other words, myInstance points to an instance (an area of memory) of MyClass on the heap.\\n\\nC++ uses pointer notation to define that:\\n\\n
\\nMyClass* myInstance = new MyClass();\\n
\\n\\nRead as: myInstance is a pointer to an instance of MyClass (on the heap).\\n\\nThat means we can create instances of MyClass that are not on the heap:\\n\\n
\\nMyClass myInstanceOnStack; //creates an instance of MyClass on the stack\\n
\\n\\nThe memory taken up by myInstanceOnStack will be freed once the method that creates this instance is out of scope.\\n\\n- So?\\n\\nIf an instance is created on the stack, we can access it directly without having to 'dereference' the pointer (this could be faster).\\n\\nIf you create an instance on the stack in a method, you should not return it from the creating method.\\n\\nLarger instances should be created on the heap because there is generally more space.\\n\\nIf you create an instance on the heap, you need to free the memory yourself (smart pointers can help here).\\n\\n\\n# Design Patterns\\nThe code touches on a number of design patterns to help with resuability:\\n\\n- Component (http://www.gameprogrammingpatterns.com/component.html)\\n\\nThe Entity class spans multiple domains (Command, Stats, EntityChildren) without coupling them to each other\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/entity/Entity.hpp].\\nIt is easy to create new and different entities with different functions (e.g. a dragon which can attack our player, or a sword which will help our player fight):\\n\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/src/Game.cpp]\\n\\nThe RenderableEntity and ControllableEntity classes are also examples. They wrap Entity with new functionality without coupling.\\n\\n- Command (http://www.gameprogrammingpatterns.com/command.html)\\n\\nThe Command class encapsulates requests as objects.\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/entity/command/Command.hpp]\\n\\nBe creating a new command implementation, users can add exciting new functionality to the game (e.g. battling dragons, opening doors).\\n\\n- State (http://www.gameprogrammingpatterns.com/state.html)\\n\\nThe game is controlled through a number of GameStates (ready, playing, won, lost, quit).\\n\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/state/GameState.hpp]\\n\\n- Observer (http://www.gameprogrammingpatterns.com/observer.html)\\n\\nThe NotificationEngine provides a 'subscriber' for observers (Notifiers) to attach to.\\n\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/engine/notification/NotificationEngine.hpp]\\n\\nDifferent Notifier implementations can choose to handle messages differently (e.g. printing text to the screen or updating the game state). \\n\\n- Strategy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategy_pattern)\\n\\nThe ControlEngine implementations provide different control strategies. One is user driven, the other AI.\\n\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/engine/control/ControlEngine.hpp]\\n\\n- Object Pool (http://www.gameprogrammingpatterns.com/object-pool.html)\\n\\nThe TextNotifier reuses an Entity to sent its messages\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/include/firstadventure/engine/notification/TextNotifier.hpp]\\n\\n# Potential Future Work\\n\\nWith code I think that the simplest solution is often the best one.\\nThere are a number of design and structural improvements which could be made to the code.\\nMost of these are marked out with TODO comments.\\nAs this is an education exercise, these improvements are beyond the scope of this project.\\n\\n### Engine and Implementation Separation.\\n\\nThe engine and implementation share the same codebase.\\n\\nIt would be exciting to package the engine as a separate product.\\n\\nUsers could easily make their own adventure games and explore the depths of their imagination.\\n\\nSee the section \\\"Tests\\\" and \\\"Entity Initialisation and Memory Management\\\" below for more details.\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\nTesting is a key aspect of developing a reusable system.\\n\\nI would go so far as to say nothing is reusable without testing:\\n\\n- If you want to resuse something, you need to know what it does; testing can answer that.\\n- If you don't have tests, how can you ensure what you are reusing works?\\n\\nAs this is an educational exercise focusing on learning C++ it was not included as part of the initial goals, however I would recommend developers devote as much time to testing as they do making their code clean and efficient.\\n\\nThe nature of the project lends itself well to adding Unit Testing and trying out some C++ frameworks.\\n\\nWe have already carried out Memory Leak testing using XCode Developer Tools.\\n\\nPerformance tests will be an interesting experiement, however optimal performance is not within the scope of this project.\\n\\n### Entity Initialisation and Memory Management\\n\\nThe game entities are initialised in the Game class as part of the initialise() method.\\n\\n[https://github.com/parisd1992/FirstAdventure/blob/master/FirstAdventure/src/Game.cpp] \\n\\nInitialisation could be simplified using an Entity Builder class.\\n\\nIt should also be possible to create the Entities (and the game itself) from a file.\\n\\nThis will make the initialising code more accessible and easier to create new adventures.\\n\\nMemory management of created Entities is challenging because they are created in the Game class initialise() method.\\n\\n4 arrays were added to Game to store the individual Entities and its Components.\\n\\nAt the end of each play, the objects in the arrays are freed and memory returned back to the heap.\\n\\nThe advantage is that the story can easily be changed by updating what is created in initialise().\\n\\nThe disadvantage is that developmers must remember to add each created Entity and Component to the respective arrays to avoid leaks.\\n\\nThe code has been tested for leaks using XCode Developer Tools. It is a personal side project but has also received some fixes from the community along the way. Bug reports and feedback are very welcome, but please check the [contributing guidelines](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) first.\\n\\n## Quick Links\\n* Play the game [here](https://nroutasuo.github.io/level13/)\\n* Read about how to report bugs, suggest features, or submit fixes to the project in the [contributing guidelines](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md)\\n* Chat about the game or get help on the [discussions page](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/discussions), the [subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/level13/), or the [Discord server](https://discord.gg/BzMbATyKph)\\n\\n## Game Overview\\n\\n### Features\\n\\n* Survival and exploration\\n* Base-building and resource-management\\n* Randomly generated maps\\n* Items, equipment and environmental hazards\\n* Technologies that slowly unlock new aspects of the game\\n\\n## Code Overview\\n\\nThe project uses [jQuery](https://jquery.com/), [Require.js](http://requirejs.org/), and [Ash.js](https://github.com/brejep/ash-js) and is structured according to an entity system framework into entities, components and systems.\\n\\n### Branches\\n* **master** is a development branch and can contain unfinished and buggy features\\n* **gh-pages** is more stable and contains whatever is currently live\\n\\n### Entities and Components\\n\\nAll game data is stored in various [Components](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/tree/master/src/game/components) that are attached to entities such as the player or a sector. Entities are simply containers for Components. The [EntityCreator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/game/EntityCreator.js) gives a good overview of what kind of entities have what kind of components.\\n\\n### Systems\\n\\nVarious independent [Systems](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/tree/master/src/game/systems) use and change data on Components and make stuff happen in the game. They generate resources, update movement options, resolve fights and so on. Each area of the UI is taken care of by its own [UI system](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/tree/master/src/game/systems/ui).\\n\\n### Player Actions\\n\\nEverything that the player can do in the game - mainly button clicks - are called \\\"player actions\\\". Each action has an associated name, costs, requirements, cooldown and so on. The [PlayerActionFunctions](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/game/PlayerActionFunctions.js) class contains a function for each action and handles their results. Various helpers take care of checking requirements, deducting costs, unifying random encounters and so on.\\n\\n### World Creator\\n\\nAt the start of a new game, a seed value is assigned to the game. The [World Creator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/tree/master/src/worldcreator) generates a unique world based on this seed and only the seed needs to be saved between sessions.\\n\\n![samplelevel2](/docs/samplelevel2.PNG) ![samplelevel3](/docs/samplelevel3.PNG)\\n\\n(Sample level structure)\\n\\nThe world is generated in roughly the following steps:\\n* [WorldGenerator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/worldcreator/WorldGenerator.js) determines rough structure of the entire world and important points like camp and passage locations\\n* [LevelGenerator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/worldcreator/LevelGenerator.js) adds more details to each level\\n* [StructureGenerator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/worldcreator/StructureGenerator.js) determines the structure of each level, placing sectors and paths according to constraints set in the previous steps\\n* [SectorGenerator](https://github.com/nroutasuo/level13/blob/master/src/worldcreator/SectorGenerator.js) populates the sectors with features like resources, item stashes, environmental hazards, movement blockers etc\\n\\nTwo important units for balancing the world are the camp ordinal and the level ordinal. Level 13 where the player always starts has level ordinal 1 and camp ordinal 1.\\n\\n## Other games\\n\\nLevel 13 is heavily inspired by [A Dark Room]( http://adarkroom.doublespeakgames.com/). Other great text-based and / or incremental games that the game owes much inspiration to include:\\n\\n* [Kittens Game](http://bloodrizer.ru/games/kittens/)\\n* [Shark Game](http://cirri.al/sharks/)\\n* [Crank](https://faedine.com/games/crank/b39/)\\n* [CivClicker](http://civclicker.sourceforge.net/civclicker/civclicker.html)\\n* [Prosperity](https://home.prosperity-game.com/)\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\",\"icon-license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-019\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":1,\".py\":4,\".md\":1},\"features\":[],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# LevPy\\n> Text-based games made easy!\\n\\n[![stable version badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/Stable-v.2.1-brightgreen)](https://github.com/flancast90/LevPy/releases/latest)[![repo size badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-2.276kb-informational)](https://www.github.com/flancast90/LevPy)\\n\\n# About \\nLevPy is a simple python file/function that allows the creation of text-based games easily through JSON data. For example, in ```main.py```, you could include the following \\\"level\\\": \\n```python\\nfirstVar = '{\\\"greeting\\\":\\\"Hello and welcome to LevPy! Type \\\\\\\"tell me more\\\\\\\" to learn more\\\",\\\"tell me more\\\":\\\"LevPy is a python library that makes making games easy!\\\"}'\\n```\\n\\n# Walk-Through/How-To\\nAs you can see, the initial JSON value ```greeting``` has the output of ```Hello and welcome ...```, and when the user types in \\\"tell me more\\\", we want LevPy to output ```LevPy is a python lib ...```. So how do we actually give the outputs and listen for the inputs? Easy, just tell the LevPy.py file what to do like so: \\n```python\\n# Change\\n# def Command1_(update): to\\ndef firstVar_(update):\\n\\n#and all of this\\n#if update != \\\"COMMAND TO SEND USER SOMEWHERE ELSE\\\":\\n# pos = \\\"CHANGE PLAYER POS\\\"\\n# mainLoop(update)\\n# else:\\n# pos = \\\"SAME POS\\\"\\n# mainLoop(update)\\n#\\n#mainLoop (\\\"COMMAND TO BEGIN WITH\\\") to\\n\\nif update != \\\"tell me more\\\":\\n print(\\\"Ended Program.\\\")\\n else:\\n pos = \\\"firstVar\\\"\\n mainLoop(update)\\n\\nmainLoop(\\\"greeting\\\")\\n```\\n\\nTo make a more advanced program, say a full-fledged game, obviously you would need much more than a single function. Instead, just set multiple variable names in ```main.py```, which LevPy will interpret as different levels or rooms. In ```LevPy.py```, you must then create functions that share the names of the variables with an underscore ```_``` added afterwards. To refer from one function to another, just update the ```pos``` value. For example, if your new JSON var was called secondVar: \\n\\n```python\\ndef firstVar_(update):\\nif update != \\\"tell me more\\\":\\n pos = \\\"secondVar\\\"\\n mainLoop(update)\\n else:\\n pos = \\\"firstVar\\\"\\n mainLoop(update)\\n\\nmainLoop(\\\"greeting\\\")\\n```\\n\\n# Contributing/Issues\\nAnyone is welcome to contribute to LevPy; It is fully community-funded and open-source. To do so, just create a Pull Request and add your wanted code. Any issues or bugs in the code, feel free to make a New Issue, and I will attempt to figure out what is going-on.\\n\\n# License \\nApache 2.0. Starting large projects in Z80 assembly language from scratch is a bit of a daunting prospect, so I decided to code the game in C first, so that I could get the design right, and avoid getting stuck in too many low-level details initially. Later I ported to the Spectrum, because it seemed like a fun challenge for myself!\\n\\nQuick links within this README file:\\n\\n* [Play Online](#play-online)\\n* [Plot of the game](#game-plot)\\n* [C Implementation](#c-implementation)\\n* [Z80 Implementation](#z80-implementation)\\n * [Z80 Changes](#z80-changes)\\n * [Memory Map](#memory-map)\\n* [Compiling & running it](#compiling--running-it)\\n* [Downloading It](#downloading-it)\\n* [Bugs?](#bugs)\\n\\n\\n\\n## Play Online\\n\\nThanks to the excellent [jsspeccy](https://github.com/gasman/jsspeccy3) ZX Spectrum emulator you can play this game with your browser here:

\\n\\n* [https://steve.fi/software/lighthouse/](https://steve.fi/software/lighthouse/)\\n\\n\\n\\n## Game Plot\\n\\n* You're inside a lighthouse (trapped? doesn't really matter I guess).\\n* You see a boat on the horizon, heading your way.\\n* But \\\"oh no!\\\", the lighthouse is dark.\\n * The boat will surely crash if you don't turn on the main light.\\n\\nThe game is over, when you either fix the light, or find another solution.\\n\\nIf you do not achieve victory within a turn-limit the boat runs aground, and\\ndeath will consume you all. (It is a _very_ big boat!)\\n\\n\\n\\n## C Implementation\\n\\nThe implementation is mostly concerned with creating the correct series of\\ndata-structures, which are essentially arrays of objects. Because if we\\ncan make the game table-based we simplify the coding that needs to be\\ndone - we don't need to write per-object handlers anywhere, we can just\\nadd pointers to tables/structures.\\n\\nThe C implementation defines most of the important things in the file [globals.h](c/globals.h) such as:\\n\\n* The structure to define a location.\\n* The structure to define an object.\\n\\nThe game-state itself is stored in a couple of global variables, there isn't\\ntoo much state to care about:\\n\\n* The current location (i.e. index into location-table).\\n* A list of any items you're carrying.\\n* The number of turns you've taken.\\n * Incremented by one each time you enter a command, be it recognized or not.\\n* Whether you won/lost.\\n\\n\\n\\n## Z80 Implementation\\n\\nThe Z80 implementation is based upon [the C-implementation](c/), with a few small changes.\\n\\nThe implementation uses a simple set of structures:\\n\\n* A command-table to map input-commands to handlers.\\n* An item-table to store details about each object in the game.\\n* A person table to store telephone messages.\\n\\nThe main implementation can be found in the file [game.z80](game.z80),\\nbut because we support two targets (CP/M 2.x and the ZX Spectrum) there\\nis a small amount of platform-specific code found in [bios.z80](bios.z80).\\n\\nThe `Makefile` should build everything appropriately for both systems,\\ndefining `SPECTRUM`, and `ENTRYPOINT` as appropriate.\\n\\n\\n### Z80 Changes\\n\\n* Along the way I realized that having fixed inventory slots made the coding more of a challenge, so I made the location of each object a property of the object itself.\\n* The Z80 version has more easter-eggs (Try typing \\\"`xyzzy`\\\" a few times).\\n* There is rudimentary support for text-wrapping.\\n * Enter `WRAP 80` to wrap output around column 80.\\n * Enter `WRAP` to view the current wrapping value.\\n* There are __two__ victory conditions.\\n* The game can be built with the text-strings, and game code, protected by simple XOR encryption:\\n * This stops users from looking through the binary for hints.\\n * Run `make release` to build both \\\"normal\\\" and \\\"protected\\\" versions of the release.\\n * The encrypted versions of the games have an X suffix in their filenames.\\n\\n\\n### Memory Map\\n\\nRoughly speaking the game consists of two parts:\\n\\n* The driver/game which is about 3k of code.\\n* The text of the game along with the state of the world (flags, items carried, etc), which is approximately 9k.\\n\\nAll told the binaries for both CP/M and the ZX Spectrum are approximately 14k.\\n\\nThe layout in memory is basically the same for both variants, however the starting address is different:\\n\\n* CP/M\\n * Game loaded between the range 256-14000\\n * [0x0100-0x3500]\\n * Copy of state made to 53248 / 0xD000\\n* ZX Spectrum\\n * Game loaded between the range 32768-46000\\n * [0x5000-0xB400]\\n * Copy of state made to 53248 - 0xD000\\n\\nWhen the game starts a copy of the \\\"state\\\" is made to `0xD000` before anything has been modified, and then when the game is started that state is copied back to where it is used. This consists of all content between `per_game_state_start` and the end of the file. This has the location, flags, and similar, as well as all the static-text which will not change between runs. However copying this region was easier than just copying, or otherwise resetting, the state that changes during play.\\n\\nNo doubt things will change over time, however the (undocumented) `BIOS` command will show you rough sizes for the various parts of the game.\\n\\n\\n\\n## Compiling & Running It\\n\\nEnsure you have the `pasmo` assembler installed, and then use the supplied Makefile to compile the game.\\n\\nRunning `make` will generate the default targets, if you wish to build only individual things then :\\n\\n* `make game-cpm` to build a normal CP/M version.\\n * `make game-cpm-encrypted` to build an encrypted CP/M version.\\n* `make game-spectrum` to build the ZX Spectrum version.\\n * `make game-spectrum-encrypted` to build the encrypted ZX Spectrum version.\\n* `make lighthouse` will build the C-game for Linux\\n* `make release` will build both versions of the CP/M and ZX Spectrum release.\\n\\nIf you have a working golang system you can run the game under this trivial CP/M emulator:\\n\\n* https://github.com/skx/cpmulator\\n\\n\\n\\n## Downloading It\\n\\nIf you look on our [release page](https://github.com/skx/lighthouse-of-doom/releases/) you can find the latest stable build.\\n\\n* For CP/M download `lihouse.com` to your system, and then run `LIHOUSE` to launch it.\\n * `lihousex.com` is the encrypted version.\\n* For the ZX Spectrum download `lihouse.tap` to your system, and then launch in your favourite emulator.\\n * `lihousex.tap` is the encrypted version.\\n\\n\\n\\n## Bugs?\\n\\nReport any bugs as you see them:\\n\\n* A crash of the game is a bug.\\n* Bad spelling, grammar, or broken punctuation are also bugs.\\n* Getting into a zombie-state where winning or losing are impossible is a bug.\\n\\n\\n\\nSteve\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-021\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":25,\".php\":584,\".md\":24,\".conf\":12,\".crt\":1,\".key\":1,\".caddyfile\":8,\".ini\":10,\".ps1\":3,\".sh\":3,\".dev\":1,\".prod\":1,\".test\":13,\".js\":76,\".yml\":5,\".iml\":1,\".xml\":30,\".xsd\":1,\".txt\":3,\".json\":5,\".css\":6,\".png\":10,\".jpg\":1,\".gif\":22,\".yaml\":158,\".lock\":2,\".html\":1076,\".phar\":1,\".dist\":1,\".ico\":1,\".properties\":1,\".sql\":11,\".twig\":166},\"features\":[\"combat\",\"quest\",\"parser\",\"command\",\"save\",\"map\",\"movement\",\"event\",\"character\",\"class\",\"skill\",\"item\",\"layer\",\"export\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"#
