\\n\\nScienceWorld is a text-based virtual environment centered around accomplishing tasks from the standardized elementary science curriculum. This code accompanies the paper [ScienceWorld: Is your Textual Agent Smarter than a 5th grader?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07540).\\n\\n

\\n\\n### Demo and examples\\n\\nYou can try ScienceWorld yourself via our [HuggingFace Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/MarcCote/ScienceWorld) or read some of the [playthrough transcripts](https://sciworld.apps.allenai.org/explore).\\n\\n### Citation\\n```\\n@inproceedings{wang-etal-2022-scienceworld,\\n title = \\\"{S}cience{W}orld: Is your Agent Smarter than a 5th Grader?\\\",\\n author = \\\"Wang, Ruoyao and\\n Jansen, Peter and\\n C{\\\\^o}t{\\\\'e}, Marc-Alexandre and\\n Ammanabrolu, Prithviraj\\\",\\n editor = \\\"Goldberg, Yoav and\\n Kozareva, Zornitsa and\\n Zhang, Yue\\\",\\n booktitle = \\\"Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing\\\",\\n month = dec,\\n year = \\\"2022\\\",\\n address = \\\"Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates\\\",\\n publisher = \\\"Association for Computational Linguistics\\\",\\n url = \\\"https://aclanthology.org/2022.emnlp-main.775/\\\",\\n doi = \\\"10.18653/v1/2022.emnlp-main.775\\\",\\n pages = \\\"11279--11298\\\",\\n}\\n```\\n\\n# Quickstart\\n**Before running:** You will have to have `Java 1.8+` installed on your system (shipped with most linux distributions) and `Python 3.8+`. We recommend creating a conda environment like this:\\n\\n```bash\\nconda create --name scienceworld python=3.8\\nconda activate scienceworld\\n```\\n\\nThen, install ScienceWorld either from PyPi:\\n\\n pip install scienceworld\\n\\nor from source in development mode:\\n\\n git clone https://github.com/allenai/ScienceWorld.git\\n cd ScienceWorld\\n pip install .\\n\\n\\nRun an example random agent, on task 13 (classification: place a non-living thing in a box), for 5 episodes:\\n\\n python examples/random_agent.py --task-num=13 --num-episodes=5 --simplifications-preset easy\\n\\nRun a user console where you can interact with the environment, on task 3 (change of state: melting):\\n\\n python examples/human.py --task-num=3 --num-episodes=5\\n\\n\\n# Web Server Demo\\n\\nA web server demo is also available, that allows running a ScienceWorld user console that can be interacted with in a web browser.\\n\\n

\\n\\nTo run the web server demo:\\n```bash\\nconda create --name scienceworld python=3.8\\nconda activate scienceworld\\npip install scienceworld[webserver]\\n```\\n\\nRun the web server:\\n\\n python examples/scienceworld-web-server-example.py\\n\\nPoint your web browser to:\\n`localhost:8080`\\n\\n\\n# ScienceWorld Design\\nScienceWorld is written in Scala (2.12.9), and compiles using `sbt` into a JAR file that is run with Java. For convenience, a Python API is provided (Python >= 3.8), which interfaces using the `py4j` package.\\n\\nIf you modified the Scala code, you can recompile the JAR file by running:\\n```bash\\n./simulator/package.sh\\npip install -e .\\n```\\n\\n# Tasks\\nThe tasks are listed in the table below along with their number of variations. Either the task ID or its name can be used to a task with `env.load()`.\\n\\n| Task ID | Task Name | # Variations |\\n|-------|----------------------------------------------------|------|\\n| 1-1 | boil | 30 |\\n| 1-2 | melt | 30 |\\n| 1-3 | freeze | 30 |\\n| 1-4 | change-the-state-of-matter-of | 30 |\\n| 2-1 | use-thermometer | 540 |\\n| 2-2 | measure-melting-point-known-substance | 436 |\\n| 2-3 | measure-melting-point-unknown-substance | 300 |\\n| 3-1 | power-component | 20 |\\n| 3-2 | power-component-renewable-vs-nonrenewable-energy | 20 |\\n| 3-3 | test-conductivity | 900 |\\n| 3-4 | test-conductivity-of-unknown-substances | 600 |\\n| 4-1 | find-living-thing | 300 |\\n| 4-2 | find-non-living-thing | 300 |\\n| 4-3 | find-plant | 300 |\\n| 4-4 | find-animal | 300 |\\n| 5-1 | grow-plant | 126 |\\n| 5-2 | grow-fruit | 126 |\\n| 6-1 | chemistry-mix | 32 |\\n| 6-2 | chemistry-mix-paint-secondary-color | 36 |\\n| 6-3 | chemistry-mix-paint-tertiary-color | 36 |\\n| 7-1 | lifespan-longest-lived | 125 |\\n| 7-2 | lifespan-shortest-lived | 125 |\\n| 7-3 | lifespan-longest-lived-then-shortest-lived | 125 |\\n| 8-1 | identify-life-stages-1 | 14 |\\n| 8-2 | identify-life-stages-2 | 10 |\\n| 9-1 | inclined-plane-determine-angle | 168 |\\n| 9-2 | inclined-plane-friction-named-surfaces | 1386 |\\n| 9-3 | inclined-plane-friction-unnamed-surfaces | 162 |\\n| 10-1 | mendelian-genetics-known-plant | 120 |\\n| 10-2 | mendelian-genetics-unknown-plant | 480 |\\n\\n## Simplifications\\nScienceWorld supports a number of simplifications that can be applied to the environment to make it easier for agents to learn. These simplifications can be applied by passing the `--simplifications-preset` argument to the command line interface, or by passing the `simplifications` argument to the Python API.\\n\\nThe available simplifications are:\\n- `teleportAction`: Allows agents to instantly move to any location in the environment.\\n- `openDoors`: All doors in the environment are open by default.\\n- `selfWateringFlowerPots`: Automatically waters all flower pots in the environment.\\n- `noElectricalAction`: Disables electrical actions, making it easier for agents to learn tasks that do not require electrical actions.\\n- `openContainers`: All containers in the environment are open by default.\\n\\nThe `--simplifications-preset` argument can be set to `easy` to apply the following simplifications:\\n- `teleportAction`\\n- `openDoors`\\n- `selfWateringFlowerPots`\\n- `noElectricalAction` (for non-connectivity tasks)\\n\\n> [!WARNING]\\n> The `easy` preset differs from what is described in the paper (see Appendix B.5). The `openContainers` is not included in that preset and should manually be added if desired.\\n\\n\\n# Baseline Agents\\n**DRRN:** https://github.com/cognitiveailab/drrn-scienceworld\\n\\n**KG-A2C:** https://github.com/cognitiveailab/kga2c-scienceworld\\n\\n**CALM:** https://github.com/cognitiveailab/calm-scienceworld\\n\\n**Behavior Cloning and Decision Transformer:** https://github.com/cognitiveailab/t5-scienceworld\\n\\n\\n\\n# Developers\\n\\nTo compile the ScienceWorld JAR file, follow these steps:\\n\\n### Prerequisites\\nYou will need to have `Java 1.8+` SDK installed on your system (shipped with most linux distributions). E.g. on Ubuntu, you can install it with:\\n\\n sudo apt-get install openjdk-21-jdk\\n\\nThen, install sbt (Scala Build Tool) by running:\\n```bash\\n echo \\\"deb https://repo.scala-sbt.org/scalasbt/debian all main\\\" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/sbt.list\\n echo \\\"deb https://repo.scala-sbt.org/scalasbt/debian /\\\" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/sbt_old.list\\n curl -sL \\\"https://keyserver.ubuntu.com/pks/lookup?op=get&search=0x2EE0EA64E40A89B84B2DF73499E82A75642AC823\\\" | sudo tee /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/sbt.asc\\n sudo apt-get update\\n sudo apt-get install sbt\\n```\\n\\n### Building the JAR\\nOnce you have `sbt` installed, you can compile the ScienceWorld JAR file by running:\\n```bash\\n./simulator/package.sh\\n```\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-030\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".yml\":1,\"\":2,\".txt\":1,\".png\":2,\".0\":2,\".md\":1,\".hpp\":12,\".h\":1,\".cpp\":13},\"features\":[\"audio\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"\\n\\n\\n**Silver C++** is a simple and easy-to-use library designed for text-based game development. \\n**Silver C++** is compatible with both **Linux-based** and **Windows-based** operating systems.\\nFor **Windows** users, you can use the [Silver Windows Edition](https://github.com/imagment/Silver-Windows-Edition/tree/dev). \\n\\n## Features \\n- \u274c **No external dependencies** - All required libraries are included into Silver C++\\n- \ud83d\ude80 **Simple & Lightweight** \u2013 Minimal setup required, so you can focus on game logic.\\n- \ud83c\udfa8 **Rich Text Support** \u2013 Easily display formatted text, colors, and simple animations for immersive gameplay. \\n- \ud83c\udfae **Interactive Input Handling** \u2013 Seamlessly process user input for interactive storytelling and decision-making. \\n- \ud83d\udee0 **Easy-to-Use API** \u2013 Intuitive functions for game logic, and essential components like transform, camera and sprite rendering. \\n- \u26a1 **Multithreading Support** \u2013 Boost performance by running tasks concurrently. \\n- \ud83d\udd22 **Math Module** \u2013 Built-in utilities for Vectors and Rects\\n- \ud83d\udcdd **Code Style** \u2013 Written in C++17 using CamelCase and PascalCase notation for clarity and consistency.\\n\\n## Examples\\n```\\n#include \\\"Silver.hpp\\\"\\n\\nint main() {\\n Actor c1;\\n c1.AddComponent();\\n\\n\\n Actor actor(\\\"alert\\\", \\\"Hello World!\\\");\\n actor.GetComponent()->position = Vector3Zero;\\n actor.GetComponent()->scale = Vector3(1,1,1);\\n \\n actor.AddObject();\\n c1.GetComponent()->RenderFrame();\\n\\n Hold();\\n return 0;\\n}\\n```\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-031\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":3,\".md\":2,\".am\":1,\".ac\":1,\".json\":2,\".txt\":7,\".hpp\":35,\".cpp\":31,\".sh\":1,\".6\":1},\"features\":[\"parser\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"save\",\"state\",\"class\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# SwannSong Adventure\\nA text-adventure game with some humor. Ill be leaving this one here for myelf to look back on and laugh, plus it's a good proof of concept.\\n\\n# Text RPG Game Engine\\n\\nVersion: 0.6.0 - AI update\\n\\nThis repository contains a game engine for a text-based RPG, written in Python. The game is mainly command-line based, but it also includes support for a GUI using Tkinter. Most game-specific information is stored in JSON files.\\n\\nKeep in mind this is an early version and a work in progress. It is not currently entirely functional. Currently, the game engine is more of an interactive world engine, and less a game.\\n\\n## Features\\n- A flexible command system that allows players to interact with the game world using natural language commands\\n- A robust system for managing game objects, including NPCs, items, and locations\\n- The ability to customize the game world using JSON files\\n- Command line & GUI capabilities\\n- Packaged in a nice executable file\\n- The option to save and load game progress\\n- Transformer (GPT) based command parser and Describer\\n\\n### Planned Features\\n- Ability to export games as executables\\n- Quests, Combat, NPC interaction (After this, it will have an actual win condition and will be released as alpha version 1.0.0)\\n- AI-assisted world generation and npc controller\\n- UI features for easy world creation and game editing\\n\\n## Requirements\\n\\n- Python 3\\n\\n### Dependencies\\n- PySimpleGUI (GUI)\\n- Art (command line)\\n- openai (GPT)\\n\\n## Usage\\n\\nTo use the game engine, clone this repository.\\n\\n`git clone https://github.com/levgrav/text-rpg.git\\ncd rpg-game-engine`\\n\\nTo customize the game, edit the JSON files in the `game_data` directory.\\n\\nTo run the game, run the `main.py` file:\\n\\n`python main.py`\\n\\nIf you want to use the GUI, in `game_data/settings.json`, make sure it says, `\\\"io_outlet\\\": \\\"gui\\\"` instead of `\\\"io_outlet\\\": \\\"terminal\\\"` and vice versa for those that want a command-line game. Likewise, if you want to use the GhatGPT parser, make sure it says, `\\\"parser_type\\\": \\\"gpt\\\"` instead of `\\\"parser_type\\\": \\\"standard\\\"` and vice versa for those that want a standard parser.\\nNote: if you want to use GPT for the parser and NPC chatbot, you will (as of yet) need to provide your own API key. I may be able to get a public version running, but it might rely on ads or donations. I hate ads though.\\n\\n## Game World\\n\\nThe informaion about the game world is located in `default_world.json`. All of the information is categorized into `\\\"areas\\\": [...]` and `\\\"npcs\\\": [...]`. In python that will look like `World.areas` and `World.npcs` which will each be a list of `Area` and `Npc` objects, respectively. \\n\\nThe game map is divided in a grid, each cell being an `Area`. Each `Area` is further subdivided into `Room`s (both if which the player can enter)\\n\\n### Areas\\n\\n`Area` objects contains the information needed for a section of the world map. \\n\\nAttributes:\\n- name\\n - `str` object that contains the name of the area.\\n- pos\\n - `list` object that contains the position of the area in the form `[x, y]`\\n- description\\n - `str` object that contains a brief description of the area.\\n- rooms\\n - `list` object that contains `Room` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n- containers\\n - `list` object that contains `Container` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n- inventory\\n - `list` object that contains `Item` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n\\n\\n### Rooms\\n\\n`Room` objects contains the information needed for a room (duh). Rooms are located inside areas and can all be accessed from anywhere inside their respective area. \\n\\nAttributes:\\n- name\\n - `str` object that contains the name of the room.\\n- description\\n - `str` object that contains a brief description of the area.\\n- containers\\n - `list` object that contains `Container` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n- inventory\\n - `list` object that contains `Item` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n\\n### Containers\\n\\n`Container` objects contains information (such as container inventory) for a container. Containers can exist both in `Area`s and `Room`s\\n\\nAttributes:\\n- name\\n - `str` object that contains the name of the area.\\n- description\\n - `str` object that contains a brief description of the area.\\n- inventory\\n - `list` object that contains `Item` objects (see below for a more detailed description).\\n\\n### Items\\nItems contain item-spcific information that is unique to each item type. For example a `Melee_Weapon` might have an attribute `base_damage`.\\n\\nSome attributes all items have in commom:\\n- name\\n - `str` object that contains the name of the item.\\n- description\\n - `str` object that contains a brief description of the item.\\n- item_type\\n - `str` object that contains the type of item, such as `'Melee_Weapon'` or `'Food'`. \\n\\n## Lisence\\n\\nMIT License (c) 2023 Levi Eby. Left by society. \\nNow you walk the streets looking for food and shelter.\\nSurvive as long as you can.\\n\\n## World\\n\\n![map](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/32639021/32135083-506a1c80-bbf9-11e7-88c8-12e6a5b39edc.png)\\n\\n\\n## In-Game Actions\\n\\n- look ? \\t\\t: looks at the current room or at the specified item in the current room\\n- inventory ? \\t: looks at the players inventory or at the specified item in the player inventory\\n- money \\t\\t\\t\\t\\t: diplays player current money\\n- hunger\\t\\t\\t\\t\\t: displays player current health\\n- beg\\t\\t\\t\\t\\t\\t: beg's the people around the player for money\\n- eat \\t\\t\\t: eat's the specified food item inside the player's inventory\\n- take \\t\\t\\t: take an item from the current room and place it in the player's inventory\\n- throw \\t\\t\\t: throw an item from the player's inventory into the current room\\n- go [north|south|east|west]: go to the specified direction\\n- open : open an item container from your inventory\\n- exit | quit\\t\\t\\t\\t: shut down the game\\n\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license.md\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-036\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".md\":1,\".txt\":1,\".exe\":1,\".dll\":3,\".rc\":2,\".cpp\":4,\".h\":3,\".ico\":2},\"features\":[\"inventory\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# Textia-RPG\\n+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n### Intro\\nConsole Text-based RPG game inspired from \\\"Sanctuary RPG: Black Edition\\\".

\\n\\nDevelopment Started in 2020.\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-037\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".yml\":4,\"\":13,\".yaml\":2,\".md\":12,\".txt\":9,\".in\":1,\".py\":122,\".json\":14,\".sh\":6,\".bat\":1,\".rst\":32,\".png\":23,\".ipynb\":4,\".z8\":8,\".toml\":1,\".twl\":63,\".twg\":19,\".ebnf\":4,\".pddl\":2,\".twl2\":1,\".handlebars\":1,\".css\":2,\".js\":4,\".i6t\":1,\".ini\":1},\"features\":[\"quest\",\"parser\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"random\",\"world\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# TextWorld\\n\\n[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/textworld.svg?logo=pypi&label=PyPI&logoColor=gold)](https://pypi.org/project/textworld)\\n[![PyPI - Python Version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/textworld.svg?logo=python&label=Python&logoColor=gold)](https://pypi.org/project/textworld/)\\n[![Build Status](https://dev.azure.com/maluuba/TextWorld/_apis/build/status/microsoft.TextWorld?branchName=main)](https://dev.azure.com/maluuba/TextWorld/_build/latest?definitionId=180&branchName=main)\\n[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/textworld/badge/?version=latest)](https://textworld.readthedocs.io/en/stable/?badge=stable)\\n[![Join the chat at https://gitter.im/Microsoft/TextWorld](https://badges.gitter.im/Microsoft/TextWorld.svg)](https://gitter.im/Microsoft/TextWorld?utm_source=badge&utm_medium=badge&utm_campaign=pr-badge&utm_content=badge)\\n\\nA text-based game generator and extensible sandbox learning environment for training and testing reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Also check out [aka.ms/textworld](https://aka.ms/textworld/) for more info about TextWorld and its creators. Have questions or feedback about TextWorld? Send them to textworld@microsoft.com or use the Gitter channel listed above.\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\nTextWorld supports __Python 3.9/3.10/3.11/3.12__ for __Linux__ and __macOS__ systems only at the moment. For __Windows__ users, docker can be used as a workaround (see Docker section below).\\n\\n### Requirements\\n\\nTextWorld requires some system libraries for its native components.\\nOn a Debian/Ubuntu-based system, these can be installed with\\n\\n sudo apt update && sudo apt install build-essential libffi-dev python3-dev curl git\\n\\nAnd on macOS, with\\n\\n brew install libffi curl git\\n\\n> **Note:** We advise our users to use virtual environments to avoid Python packages from different projects to interfere with each other. Popular choices are [Conda Environments](https://conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html) and [Virtualenv](https://virtualenv.pypa.io/en/stable/)\\n\\n### Installing TextWorld\\n\\nThe easiest way to install TextWorld is via [`pip`](https://pypi.org/):\\n\\n pip install textworld\\n\\nOr, after cloning the repo, go inside the root folder of the project (i.e. alongside `setup.py`) and run\\n\\n pip install .\\n\\n#### Visualization\\n\\nTextWorld comes with some tools to visualize game states. Make sure all dependencies are installed by running\\n\\n pip install textworld[vis]\\n\\nThen, you will need to install either the [Chrome](https://sites.google.com/a/chromium.org/chromedriver/) or [Firefox](https://github.com/mozilla/geckodriver) webdriver (depending on which browser you have currently installed).\\nIf you have Chrome already installed you can use the following command to install chromedriver\\n\\n pip install chromedriver_installer\\n\\nCurrent visualization tools include: `take_screenshot`, `visualize` and `show_graph` from [`textworld.render`](https://textworld.readthedocs.io/en/latest/textworld.render.html).\\n\\n### Docker\\n\\nA docker container with the latest TextWorld release is available on [DockerHub](https://hub.docker.com/).\\n\\n docker pull marccote19/textworld\\n docker run -p 8888:8888 -it --rm marccote19/textworld\\n\\nThen, in your browser, navigate to the Jupyter notebook's link displayed in your terminal. The link should look like this\\n\\n http://127.0.0.1:8888/?token=8d7aaa...e95\\n\\n> **Note:** See [README.md](docker/README.md) in the docker folder for troubleshooting information.\\n\\n## Usage\\n\\n### Generating a game\\n\\nTextWorld provides an easy way of generating simple text-based games via the `tw-make` script. For instance,\\n\\n tw-make custom --world-size 5 --nb-objects 10 --quest-length 5 --seed 1234 --output tw_games/custom_game.z8\\n\\nwhere `custom` indicates we want to customize the game using the following options: `--world-size` controls the number of rooms in the world, `--nb-objects` controls the number of objects that can be interacted with (excluding doors) and `--quest-length` controls the minimum number of commands that is required to type in order to win the game. Once done, the game `custom_game.z8` will be saved in the `tw_games/` folder.\\n\\n### Playing a game (terminal)\\n\\nTo play a game, one can use the `tw-play` script. For instance, the command to play the game generated in the previous section would be\\n\\n tw-play tw_games/custom_game.z8\\n\\n> **Note:** Only Z-machine's games (*.z1 through *.z8) are supported.\\n\\nTo visualize the game state while playing, use the `--viewer [port]` option.\\n\\n tw-play tw_games/custom_game.z8 --viewer\\n\\nA new browser tab should open and track your progress in the game.\\n\\n### Playing a game (Python + [Gym](https://github.com/openai/gym)-like API)\\n\\nHere's how you can interact with a text-based game from within Python using a Gym-like API.\\n\\n```python\\nimport textworld.gym\\n\\n# Register a text-based game as a new environment.\\nenv_id = textworld.gym.register_game(\\\"tw_games/custom_game.z8\\\",\\n max_episode_steps=50)\\n\\nenv = textworld.gym.make(env_id) # Start the environment.\\n\\nobs, infos = env.reset() # Start new episode.\\nenv.render()\\n\\nscore, moves, done = 0, 0, False\\nwhile not done:\\n command = input(\\\"> \\\")\\n obs, score, done, infos = env.step(command)\\n env.render()\\n moves += 1\\n\\nenv.close()\\nprint(\\\"moves: {}; score: {}\\\".format(moves, score))\\n```\\n\\n> **Note:** To play text-based games without a Gym-like API, see [Playing text-based games with TextWorld.ipynb](notebooks/Playing%20text-based%20games%20with%20TextWorld.ipynb)\\n\\n## Documentation\\n\\nFor more information about TextWorld, check the [documentation](https://aka.ms/textworld-docs).\\n\\n## Visual Studio Code\\n\\nYou can install the [textworld-vscode extension ](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=textworld.textworld-vscode) that enables syntax highlighting for editing `.twl` and `.twg` TextWorld files.\\n\\n## Notebooks\\n\\nCheck the [notebooks](notebooks) provided with the framework to see what you can do with it. You will need the [Jupyter Notebook](https://jupyter.org/install) to run them. Library Tests](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdor-pp/workflows/Core%20Library%20Tests/badge.svg)\\n\\n# Trogdor++\\n\\nA batteries-included engine with tools for building single and multi-player text adventures and MUDs.\\n\\n## Introduction\\n\\nTrogdor++ provides you with all the tools you need to build a solid interactive fiction experience, from offline single-player text adventures to massive online MUDs and everything in-between.\\n\\nAt the heart of Trogdor++ is the core library, implemented in this repository, written in C++. This library supports all the basic features necessary to build a basic game out of the box with no programming required. For features that aren't baked into the library itself, Trogdor++ also includes bindings that make it straightforward to extend using both Lua and C++.\\n\\nTrogdor++ is a work in progress and more features are being added all the time.\\n\\n## Overview\\n\\nThe Trogdor++ project consists of the following components:\\n\\n* [Core](src/core/README.md): The core library, written in C++\\n* [Standalone](src/standalone/README.md): A barebones single-player CLI client, written primarily as a demonstration for how to use the library\\n* [Trogdord](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdord): A queryable TCP server capable of hosting multi-player games with configurable crash recovery features and optional support for [Redis Pub/Sub](https://redis.io/topics/pubsub)\\n* [The official PHP 7/8 trogdord extension](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdord_php): A client for trogdord that's built into PHP\\n* [The official Node.js trogdord module](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdord_nodejs): A Node.js client for trogdord\\n\\nDescriptions of each component, along with build instructions, can be found by clicking the links above.\\n\\n## How it Works\\n\\nAt a high level, the modules in this project are built to work together in the following configurations:\\n\\n### Standalone Single-Player Games\\n\\n![Single-Player Configuration](./docs/img/how-it-works/single-player.png)\\n\\nIn this configuration, a client application links against the core library in order to drive games with a single player. In [src/standalone](src/standalone/README.md), you'll find a C++ application demonstrating this use case. This is what you would prefer if you wanted to write a simple console-based text adventure.\\n\\nAt the moment, this isn't intended for actual use but to serve as an example for how you might go about building your own single player application. I intend to build this out more fully in the future, but for now, most of my attention is directed toward improving the multi-player aspects of the engine.\\n\\n### Hosted Multi-Player Games\\n\\nTrogdor++ includes an optional TCP server ([src/trogdord](src/trogdord/README.md)) capable of hosting many multi-player games in parallel. There are a few different ways this can be configured, each of which is outlined below.\\n\\n#### Trogdord Without Redis\\n\\n![Multi-Player Configuration Without Redis](./docs/img/how-it-works/multi-player-no-redis.png)\\n\\nHere, input and output pass directly through trogdord. To actually host games would require polling for output and wouldn't be very efficient, but it's easy to setup and is useful for testing and other one-off tasks. Note that querying trogdord directly is still possible even when using the Redis configuration described below.\\n\\n#### Trogdord With Redis\\n\\n![Multi-Player Configuration With Redis](./docs/img/how-it-works/multi-player-redis.png)\\n\\nWith this setup, trogdord will send output to a [Redis Pub/Sub](https://redis.io/topics/pubsub) channel, which will then be consumed by one or more clients. Input and other requests to the game server will, meanwhile, flow directly from one or more clients back to trogdord.\\n\\nAn example of this pattern in action is my sister project, [Trogserve](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogserve). In that case, there's a [WebSocket](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API) server on the backend that subscribes to the configured Redis channel for output, forwarding it to the browser, and receives input from the browser, sending it to trogdord via a request.\\n\\n### Other Configurations\\n\\nOther configurations are, of course, possible. You could host single player games online via trogdord, or support multi-player games locally through a custom executable with multiple input devices. You can link any application to core for any purpose; what you choose to do with it is limited only by your imagination!\\n\\n## Experimental Inform 7 Support\\n\\nAs a programming exercise, I've been working on support for [Inform 7](http://inform7.com/). It's a tricky endeavor, not only because Inform 7 is closed source (at the moment, although that's supposed to change [someday](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=20421189)), but because Inform 7 and Trogdor++ don't share all the same goals (Inform 7 compiles down to [Inform 6](https://inform-fiction.org/), which in turn compiles down to [Z-Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-machine), and is only for single player games, while Trogdor++ uses higher level primitives and supports more than one player) and because Inform 7 supports features that don't yet exist or have been implemented differently in Trogdor++.\\n\\nThe subset of the language that I currently parse is too limited to be useful, so trogdord won't even try to open games that are written in it. However, if you want to play with the parser and see what it can do, the standalone client is equipped to load single-file Inform 7 games.\\n\\nTo read more about what I currently support, including an EBNF of the limited grammar my parser understands, take a look at [src/core/include/trogdor/parser/parsers/inform7parser.h](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdor-pp/blob/master/src/core/include/trogdor/parser/parsers/inform7parser.h).\\n\\n## Copyright and License\\n\\nTrogdor++ is licensed under the [GPL 3.0](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.en.html) and is Copyright \u00a9 2013 - Present by James Colannino.\\n\\n## History\\n\\nTrogdor++ is the C++ version of the [Trogdor Text Adventure Engine](https://github.com/crankycyclops/trogdor \\\"Trogdor Text Adventure Engine\\\"), originally written in C. That project is no longer maintained but still exists on GitHub (in an archived state) for historical purposes.\\n\\n**Fun fact:** the name Trogdor comes from [this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=90X5NJleYJQ) :)\\n\\nHave fun!\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-040\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":2,\".yaml\":1,\".py\":4,\".txt\":2,\".json\":2,\".md\":1},\"features\":[\"save\",\"character\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# TRPG\\nGeneral Menus |Battle System\\n:------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:\\n![](https://i.imgur.com/9CThK5e.gif) |![](https://i.imgur.com/GKfgAOd.gif)\\n\\nSimple Python text-based RPG that can be played on the terminal. Before running the game, install all the requirements with the command (only necessary the first time):\\n```\\n$ pip3 install -r requirements.txt\\n```\\nWhen all the requirements are installed, the command to run the game is:\\n```\\n$ python3 TRPG.py\\n```\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-041\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".md\":3,\".yml\":1,\"\":2,\".code-snippets\":1,\".py\":1,\".css\":2,\".jpg\":2,\".exe\":1,\".js\":3,\".map\":1,\".html\":2,\".bat\":3,\".json\":3,\".ts\":25},\"features\":[\"quest\",\"inventory\",\"save\",\"map\",\"item\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# VeinIF\\nVeinIF is a framework for creating choice-based Interactive Fiction game.\\\\\\nThis project uses TypeScript, HTML (& CSS)! \\\\\\n\\\\\\n[See a sample game made using VeinIF.](https://uyen18827.github.io/VeinIF-Demo/)\\n## Features\\nOut of the box, VeinIF offers:\\n\\n- Inventory System: Picking up items, loosing items and locking certain choices if items aren't in the player's inventory.\\n\\n- Attribute System: Player attributes increase or decrease depends on their choices. Choices can also be locked if certain atrribute is less than required.\\n\\n- Name & Pronouns: Built in functions that handle custom character name and pronouns.\\n\\n- Multiple save slots: Save anytime, at any point of the game. Choose between saving in the browser's localStorage or export a copy to player's local machine that can be loaded again in other browsers/devices.\\n\\nFor more informations, please refer to [the documentation](https://uyen18827.gitbook.io/veinif/features).\\n\\n## Setting up\\nPlease make sure that Node.js is installed in your machine and a copy of VeinIF is present.\\\\\\nNavigate to the folder and run the following command:\\n```\\nnpm install\\n```\\n## Development\\nUser can use the command line to run commands, or use `buildGUI.exe` to conveniently run commands.\\n## Commands\\nRun the development environment server:\\n```\\nnpm run dev\\n```\\nBuild the project for web distribution:\\n```\\nnpm run build\\n```\\nBuild a Window, stand-alone executable copy of your game:\\n```\\nnpm run electron-build\\n```\\n## Support\\nFor bug report, additional support, other inquiries and feature request, please [create an issue](https://github.com/uyen18827/VeinIF/issues/new/choose) using the provided template.\\n\\nCheck out planned features and fixes in the [Project tab](https://github.com/uyen18827/VeinIF/projects).\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-042\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":1,\".md\":1,\".gif\":1,\".rb\":1},\"features\":[\"3d\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"```\\n .~`'888x.!**h.-``888h. x .d88' oec :\\n dX `8888 :X 48888> u. 5888R @88888 u. u.\\n '888x 8888 X88. goals:\\n\\n* Lean and mean: all code should be contained in a single source file.\\n* Cross-platform: it should work reasonably well across Linux, Mac, and yes, even Windows.\\n* Instructive: the code should be clean, readable, and easy to follow.\\n* Stand-alone: No external dependencies, other than the Ruby core and standard libraries.\\n* No bitmap graphics: everything uses ASCII art and terminal colors!\\n\\nWolfentext is proudly (if not somewhat arbitrarily) written in pure Ruby.\\n\\nDocumentation may be derived from the code using the popular YARD documentation format.\\n\\nFeatures\\n========\\n\\n![Preview](preview.gif)\\n\\nHere are the features currently supported in Wolfentext:\\n\\n* Solid, orthogonal walls\\n* Recessed horizontal sliding doors\\n* Solid floor and ceiling background\\n* Textured floors and ceilings\\n* Collision detection with wall sliding\\n* Multi-directional pushwalls and moving walls\\n* Title, help, debug, and ending screens\\n* Over 16 colors of pixelated eye candy!\\n\\n...and here are some **missing** features that are still in the works:\\n\\n* [Stationary and usable objects](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/5)\\n* [Enemies and other entities](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/4)\\n* [Sounds and/or music](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/6)\\n* [Resizeable viewport](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/7)\\n* [Terminal type detection](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/8)\\n\\nRequirements\\n============\\n\\nThe only requirement for Wolfentext is a local installation of **Ruby 2.0.0+**.\\n\\nWolfentext should also work on all recent versions of OS X, Linux, and Windows. *(That said, Windows users may notice some issues when running Wolfentext in color mode. See the notes below for more information.)*\\n\\nInstallation\\n============\\n\\nTo install Wolfentext, simply download the `wolfentext.rb` file or clone the repo to your local machine:\\n\\n```\\n$ git clone http://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d.git\\n```\\n\\nUsage\\n=====\\n\\nTo start enjoying Wolfentext's pixelated goodness, command thine terminal thusly:\\n\\n```\\n$ cd wolfentext\\n$ ruby wolfentext.rb\\n```\\n\\nCompatibility\\n=============\\n\\nWolfentext has been tested against the following terminals and platforms:\\n\\n| Terminal | Platform | B/W performance | Color performance |\\n|----------------|--------------|----------------:|------------------:|\\n| Command Prompt | Windows 7 | 30-45 fps | 0-15 fps |\\n| ConEmu | Windows 7 | Not yet tested | Not yet tested |\\n| Cygwin | Windows 7 | Not yet tested | Not yet tested |\\n| GNOME Terminal | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 0-15 fps |\\n| Guake | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 45-60 fps |\\n| iTerm | Mac OS X | Not yet tested | Not yet tested |\\n| Konsole | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 45-60 fps |\\n| PowerShell | Windows 7 | 30-45 fps | 0-15 fps |\\n| Tilda | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 0-15 fps |\\n| tmux | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 45-60 fps |\\n| XTerm | Ubuntu 14.04 | 45-60 fps | 0-15 fps |\\n| Z shell (zsh) | Mac OS X | 45-60 fps | 45-60 fps |\\n\\nAlthough most modern terminal emulators seem capable of delivering playable frame rates, it goes without saying that users with integrated or low-end graphics cards may experienced decreased (and in some cases, unplayable) performance. I have noticed this myself when testing various terminal emulators on my main system: a 2010 HP Pavilion dv7 laptop with hybrid ATI graphics. *Some terminals performed over 100-200% faster when using the discrete ATI graphics card instead of the integrated Intel 915 chipset.*\\n\\n**If you are experiencing degraded or unplayable performance with Wolfentext in your favorite terminal program,** try adjusting the graphics properties of your host system (including switching to a discrete graphics mode, if your system supports it). Using the table above as a guide, you can also try running Wolfentext in another terminal emulator which may yield better performance.\\n\\nFinally, help us keep this table updated with the latest information! If you experience results different from these, please let us know by [filing an issue](http://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/) in the tracker.\\n\\nIssues\\n======\\n\\nDespite it's shimmering textiness, Wolfentext ain't perfect. Here are some known issues with the game of which you should be aware:\\n\\n* *Graphics*: In order to maintain code readability and cross-platform compatibility, Wolfentext uses a simple, single-buffered, terminal-based graphics system. In non-color mode, this should work quite well across all platforms, often achieving frame rates up to 60 fps. However, some users may notice **significant** performance issues when using *any* color mode in their preferred terminal (see Compatibility section above). Other third-party terminals may yield better performance but have not yet been tested.\\n\\n* *Input*: The input logic only handles one keypress at a time. Support for multiple keypresses is planned in a future release, assuming we can find a sensible cross-platform method that works.\\n\\n* *Terminal*: At present, the code assumes you are running this script in a compatible terminal. Logic should be added that detects not only the current terminal upon program start, but also what features are presently available to that terminal and whether they are compatible with the current version of Wolfentext.\\n\\n* *Optimizations*: Although the script utilizes several optimizations in key areas, the code could still benefit from (1) further graphical optimizations for common, low-performing terminal configurations; (2) reducing and/or eliminating the amount of floating-point math used across game calculations and lookup tables (with additional benchmarking to prove which optimizations are the most beneficial); and (3) optimizing any other remaining areas of the core ray casting engine, which presently consumes most of the processing time for each game loop iteration. Other areas of opportunity may also exist which have not yet been identified.\\n\\nAny suggestions for solving these issues are always welcome! See the Contributing section below.\\n\\nContributing\\n============\\n\\nPull requests that fix bugs or propose new functionality are always welcome, provided contributors keep the following conditions in mind:\\n\\n* Code contributions should be properly formatted and fully documented before final submissions are merged into master. If I make formatting changes to your code or request that you make similar changes yourself, please don't take it personally: the goal is to maintain a simple but consistent style across the entire project that is both readable and maintainable by others in the future. :-)\\n\\n* Before submitting new feature requests, it is recommended that you check the list of [open roadmap tickets](https://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/labels/roadmap) to see if anyone else is already working on that feature. This will help reduce the chance of duplicating efforts while allowing everyone to collaborate on the same feature more effectively.\\n\\n* All contributors whose pull requests are accepted will be given full credit for their ideas and/or submissions in the project README.\\n\\n* Since this project is officially [\\\"unlicensed\\\"](http://unlicense.org/) as public domain software, all contributors will need to agree to the following snippet and include it as a separate comment in their pull request before their contributions can be merged into the repository:\\n\\n```\\nI dedicate any and all copyright interest in this software to the\\npublic domain. I make this dedication for the benefit of the public at\\nlarge and to the detriment of my heirs and successors. I intend this\\ndedication to be an overt act of relinquishment in perpetuity of all\\npresent and future rights to this software under copyright law.\\n```\\n\\nIf you have any questions about this process, please let me know!\\n\\nSupport\\n=======\\n\\nIf you have any problems or suggestions, please let me know by [filing an issue](http://github.com/AtomicPair/wolfentext3d/issues/) in the tracker.\\n\\nHistory\\n=======\\n\\nWolfentext was originally born from the need to share a code sample with a potential recruiter. The sample had to be contained within a single file, and since I didn't have any public samples available at the time that I felt comfortable sharing, I spent the next few days creating the first iteration of Wolfentext from scratch. Since then, the script has taken on a life of it's own: adding new features, fixing bugs, and morphing into an homage to the classic 2.5D shooters from the days of my youth.\\n\\nFor the curious, here's a short summary table highlighting various milestones from past releases:\\n\\n| Release | Notable features |\\n|---------|-------------------------------------------------|\\n| 0.9.1 | Updated licensing and contributor information |\\n| 0.9.0 | Ceiling and floor textures |\\n| | In-game system messages |\\n| 0.8.0 | Wall textures |\\n| 0.7.0 | Multi-direction pushwalls |\\n| | Multi-direction moving walls |\\n| | Directionally colored walls (light/dark) |\\n| 0.6.0 | Sliding doors |\\n| 0.5.1 | Player strafing support |\\n| 0.3.0 | REAL non-blocking game loop and input system |\\n| 0.2.0 | Improved graphic system with almost no flicker |\\n| 0.1.0 | Initial alpha release |\\n\\nLicense\\n=======\\n\\nThis is free and unencumbered software released into the public domain.\\n\\nAnyone \",\"licenseIndicators\":[]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-043\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".yml\":2,\"\":3,\".md\":1,\".c\":33,\".dat\":1,\".6\":1,\".h\":3,\".txt\":1},\"features\":[\"room\",\"story\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"```\\nWelcome to Dungeon. This version created 11-MAR-91.\\nYou are in an open field west of a big white house with a boarded front door.\\nThere is a small mailbox here.\\n>\\n```\\n\\n# DUNGEON (AKA Zork)\\n\\n**Public Domain Source Code for the Mainframe Game \\\"Dungeon\\\"**\\n\\nThis repository contains the Public Domain source code for *Dungeon*, the mainframe version of the game that served as the precursor to Infocom's commercial *Zork* trilogy.\\nThis codebase is a C port derived from the FORTRAN source of **Zork 2.6**.\\n\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\n### Fedora Linux\\n\\nThis package is available in the official Fedora Linux repositories.\\nYou can install it directly via the command-line:\\n\\n```bash\\nsudo dnf install zork\\n```\\n\\n### Building from Source\\n\\nTo build the game from the source files in this repository:\\n\\n```bash\\nmake\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Modern Maintainership & Philosophy (2013-12 to present)\\n\\n**Current Maintainers:**\\n\\n* Shane Thomas ([@devshane](https://github.com/devshane))\\n* Jan Dr\u00f6gehoff ([@Jan200101](https://github.com/Jan200101))\\n* Justin Wheeler ([@justwheel](https://github.com/justwheel))\\n\\n**Project Philosophy:**\\n\\nThis project utilizes the FORTRAN source of *Dungeon* (Zork 2.6) as its foundation.\\nThe primary design goal is code preservation.\\nWe aim to maintain the logic and behavior of the game as accurately as possible while updating the codebase to compile and run on modern C compilers and operating systems.\\n\\n\\n## History of the Implementation\\n\\nThis version of *Dungeon* has been modified from FORTRAN to C.\\nThe historical lineage of this code is as follows:\\n\\n1. **Original Development (MDL)**:\\n The original game (initially titled *Zork*) was written in the MDL programming language (MUDDLE) at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science.\\n2. **PDP-11 Translation (FORTRAN)**:\\n Bob Supnik translated the MDL source into DEC FORTRAN for the PDP-11, renaming the game *Dungeon*.\\n3. **UNIX Port (f77)**:\\n The FORTRAN version was subsequently ported to `f77` for UNIX systems.\\n4. **C Translation**:\\n The C translation was generated from the `f77` version using `f2c`.\\n `f2c` is a FORTRAN-to-C translator written by David Gay (AT&T Bell Labs), Stu Feldman (Bellcore), Mark Maimone (Carnegie-Mellon University), and Norm Schryer (AT&T Bell Labs).\\n\\n*Note on Zork I:*\\nWhile often conflated, *Dungeon* differs from *Zork I*.\\n*Zork I* is a microcomputer adaptation comprising approximately one-third of the original mainframe game's map and puzzles.\\n*Dungeon* represents the more complete, albeit earlier, mainframe experience.\\n\\n### I. From original game documentation\\n\\nTo: Dungeon Players\\nFrom: \\\"The Translator\\\"\\nSubj: Game Information\\nDate: 8-OCT-80\\n\\n\\nThis is the first (and last) source release of the PDP-11 version of \\nDungeon.\\n\\nPlease note that Dungeon has been superceded by the game ZORK(tm).\\nThe following is an extract from the new product announcement for\\nZORK in the September, 1980 issue of the RT-11 SIG newsletter:\\n\\n \\\"'ZORK: The Great Underground Empire - Part I' ...was developed\\n by the original authors based on their ZORK (Dungeon) game for\\n the PDP-10. It features a greatly improved parser; command\\n input and transcript output files; SAVEs to any device and\\n file name; and adaptation to different terminal types,\\n including a status line on VT100s. Note: this is not the\\n FORTRAN version that has been available through DECUS. This\\n version has been completely rewritten to run efficiently on\\n small machines - up to 10 times as fast as the DECUS version.\\n\\n ...ZORK runs under RT-ll, HT-ll, or RSTS/E and requires as\\n little as 20K words of memory and a single floppy disk drive.\\n The game package, consisting of an RX01-format diskette and\\n an instruction booklet, is available from Infocom, Inc.,\\n P.O. Box 120, Kendall Station, Cambridge, Ma. 02142.\\\"\\n\\nZORK(tm) is a trademark of Infocom, Inc. It is available for several\\npopular personal computers as well as for the PDP-ll.\\n\\n### II. DEC FORTRAN to f77 Conversion (1981-11-17)\\n\\nThe conversion from DEC FORTRAN to Unix f77 was done by **Randy Dietrich, Lynn Cochran and Sig Peterson**.\\nMuch hacking was done to get it to fit in the limited address space of a PDP-11/44 (split I/D).\\nSuffice it to say that by leaving out the debugging package and not linking in the f77 i/o library, they managed to get it to run.\\n\\n### III. PDP to VAX (1985-12)\\n\\nBased on the work of Randy, Lynn and Sig, **Bill Randle** folded in the full save/restore functions and the game debugging package (gdt) into the PDP version to create a Vax/Unix version.\\nThis version also uses f77 i/o, thus eliminating the extra speak and listen processes needed on the PDP.\\n\\n### IV. Cleanup I (1986-12-11)\\n\\n**John Gilmore** (hoptoad!gnu) cleaned up the source files by moving most of the common declarations into include files and added comments from the original (_FORTRAN or MDL?_) source.\\nHis efforts are greatly appreciated.\\n\\n### V. Cleanup II (1987-02-09)\\n\\n**Bill Randle** added the PDP dependencies back into the Vax source files with `#ifdef`s in order to have just one set of sources.\\nPreviously, there were two sets of source: one for the PDP and one for the Vax.\\nIn addition, a shell escape of the form `!cmd` was added and the wizard can enter the gdt without having to recompile the source.\\nFinally, a man page was generated, based on the `dungeon.doc` file.\\n\\n### VI. f77 to C (1991-03-11)\\n\\n**Ian Lance Taylor** used the `f2c` translator to generate C source code.\\nThe resulting code was modified to remove the FORTRAN I/O library, to add simple more processing, and to change the format of the database file.\\n**Andre Srinivasan** helped test it.\\n**Jonathan Mark** made it work under MS-DOS and Microsoft C.\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[]}]}");

export default JSON.parse("{\"schema\":\"ai-brain-reference-analysis/1.0\",\"domain\":\"game-design\",\"capabilities\":[\"interactive-fiction\",\"command-routing\",\"state-machines\",\"combat\",\"inventory\",\"npc\",\"quest\",\"save-state\"],\"provenance\":{\"sourceType\":\"provided-reference-archives\",\"method\":\"file-structure and README capability extraction; third-party source code not redistributed\"},\"records\":[{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-001\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":1,\".sln\":1,\".h\":49,\".cpp\":9,\".vcxproj\":1,\".filters\":1,\".json\":1,\".md\":1,\".psd\":2},\"features\":[\"npc\",\"room\",\"inventory\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"

\\n

Octo-Spork

\\n \\n \\n \\n

\\n\\n### About\\n\\nOcto-Spork is a text-based adventure game I created for my assignment at University (Level 5). The story is that you are trapped inside an unknown building with three spirits blocking the path. You must search around the building to find a way to get out.\\n\\n### Code Explanation\\n\\nOcto-Spork is coded in C++ and meant to be run inside a console. The game, it's rooms and it's items are all loaded from \\\"Octo-Spork/Octo-Spork/resources/game.json\\\". [RapidJSON](https://rapidjson.org/) is being used to parse the json and extract the data into memory for being used. [OctoSpork.cpp](https://github.com/JoshLmao/Octo-Spork/blob/master/Octo-Spork/Octo-Spork/OctoSpork.cpp) also contains specific code for triggering the specific ending. However, you can change the game.json file to have extra or less rooms/items/npc's\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-002\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":5,\".yml\":2,\".md\":1,\".txt\":3,\".png\":1,\".gif\":1,\".cpp\":2,\".h\":1},\"features\":[\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# Adrift - a text adventure game\\n\\nA little game I wrote during my first year of coding. \\nA good way to learn git and C++.\\n\\n### How to run the game:\\nPull and run the 2.4MB Docker image: \\n`docker run -it --rm ghcr.io/mitchfen/adrift:latest`\\n\\n### Gameplay\\n\\n![adrift gif](./screenshots/adrift_gif.gif)\\n\\n\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-003\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":3,\".yml\":1,\".md\":2,\".gif\":1,\".clj\":12,\".js\":11,\".cljc\":18,\".cljs\":5},\"features\":[\"quest\",\"room\",\"map\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# advenjure [![Build Status](https://secure.travis-ci.org/facundoolano/advenjure.png)](http://travis-ci.org/facundoolano/advenjure)\\n\\n![Example game](example.gif)\\n\\nAdvenjure is a text adventure (or interactive fiction) game engine. I wrote it as an excuse to learn Clojure.\\nSome of its distinctive features are:\\n\\n * Target the terminal and the browser with the same codebase.\\n * Unix-like prompt with smart tab completion and command history\\n * Customizable verbs and plugins.\\n * LucasArts inspired dialog trees.\\n\\n## Example game\\n\\nYou can see the code for a working example in the [advenjure-example](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example) repository and play it online [here](https://facundoolano.github.io/advenjure).\\n\\nFor a fully fledged game see [House Taken Over](https://github.com/facundoolano/house-taken-over).\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\nAdd the following to your project map as a dependency:\\n\\n```clojure\\n[advenjure \\\"0.9.0\\\"]\\n```\\n\\n## Basic Usage\\n\\n### Creating items\\n\\nText adventures consist mainly of moving around rooms and interacting with items\\nthrough verb commands such as GO, LOOK, TAKE, etc.\\n\\nItems are represented by maps in advenjure. the `advenjure.items/make`\\nfunction takes a name, a description and a set of key-value pairs to customize behavior.\\nFor example:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.items :as items])\\n\\n(def magazine (items/make \\\"magazine\\\"\\n \\\"The cover read 'Sports Almanac 1950-2000'\\\"\\n :take true\\n :read \\\"Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0? Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0!?\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nThat will define a magazine item that can be taken (put in the player's inventory)\\nand can be read (which differs from looking at it).\\n\\nYou can provide a vector of names so the player can refer to it by one of its synonyms;\\nthe first name in the vector will be considered its canonical name:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def magazine (items/make [\\\"magazine\\\" \\\"sports magazine\\\" \\\"newspaper\\\"]\\n \\\"The cover read 'Sports Almanac 1950-2000'\\\"\\n :take true\\n :read \\\"Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0? Oh l\u00e0 l\u00e0!?\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nLike `:take` and `:read` there are keywords for the other actions\\n(`:look-at`, `:open`, `:close`, `:unlock`, etc.).\\n\\nA special kind of items are those that can contain other items:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def magazine (items/make \\\"bag\\\" :items #{magazine} :closed true))\\n```\\n\\nThe bag contains the magazine, but since it's `:closed` the player needs to open it\\nbefore being able to look inside it and take its contents. Note that marking an\\nobject as `:closed` also implies that OPEN and CLOSE verbs can be applied to it\\n(i.e. it means `:open true, :close true`).\\n\\n### Creating rooms\\n\\nOnce you've created a bunch of items, you'll need to put them in a room (if not directly\\ninto the player's inventory). Rooms are also maps and also have an\\n`advenjure.rooms/make` function to build them:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.rooms :as rooms])\\n\\n(def bedroom (rooms/make \\\"Bedroom\\\"\\n \\\"A smelling bedroom.\\\"\\n :initial-description \\\"I woke up in a smelling little bedroom, without windows.\\\"))\\n```\\n\\nNote that rooms can have only one name. `:initial-description` is an optional attribute\\nto define how the player will describe a room the first time he visits it,\\nusually with a more verbose description. If `:initial-description` is not defined,\\nand whenever the LOOK AROUND command is entered, the regular description will be used.\\n\\nTo add items to a room use `advenjure.rooms/add-item`:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def bedroom (-> (rooms/make \\\"Bedroom\\\"\\n \\\"A smelling bedroom.\\\"\\n :initial-description \\\"I woke up in a smelling little bedroom, without windows.\\\")\\n (rooms/add-item (items/make \\\"bed\\\" \\\"It was the bed I slept in.\\\"))\\n (rooms/add-item magazine \\\"On the floor was a sports magazine.\\\")))\\n```\\n\\nThe second parameter is an optional room-specific description of the item. It will be used\\nto mention the item while describing the room (as opposed of the default `a is here.`).\\n\\n### Building a room map\\n\\nOnce you have some rooms, you need to connect them to build a room map, which is\\nnothing but a plain clojure hash map. First map the room to some id keyword,\\nthen connect the rooms using the `advenjure.rooms/connect` function:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(def room-map (-> {:bedroom bedroom\\n :living living\\n :outside outside}\\n (rooms/connect :bedroom :north :living)\\n (rooms/connect :living :east :outside)))\\n```\\n\\nAn alternative function, `advenjure.rooms/one-way-connect`, allows connecting the\\nrooms just in one direction.\\n\\n### Building and running a game\\n\\nThe next building block is the game map itself, which contains the room map,\\nthe player's inventory and a pointer to the current room. `advenjure.game/make`\\nhelps to build it:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(require '[advenjure.game :as game])\\n\\n(game/make room-map :bedroom)\\n```\\n\\nThe room keyword defines what room the player will be in when the game starts.\\nIf you want to start off the game with some items in the player's inventory,\\njust pass them in a set as the third argument.\\n\\nLastly, the `advenjure.game/run` takes a game state map, a boolean function\\nto tell if the game has finished and an optional string to print before it starts.\\nPutting it all together in a `-main` function:\\n\\n```clojure\\n(defn -main\\n \\\"Build and run the game.\\\"\\n [& args]\\n (let [game-state (game/make room-map :bedroom)\\n finished? #(= (:current-room %) :outside)]\\n (game/run game-state finished? :start-message \\\"Welcome to the advenjure!\\\")))\\n```\\n\\nThe game flows by taking the initial game state map, prompting the user for a command,\\napplying the command to produce a new game state and repeat the process until the\\n`finished?` condition is met, which, in the example above means entering the\\n`:outside` room.\\n\\n## Advanced Usage\\n\\nThere is a number of advanced features available in the engine:\\n\\n * Overriding messages: use custom messages for a given action on a room or item.\\n * Pre conditions: function hook to define whether an action can be performed.\\n * Post conditions: function hook to customize how the game state is modified after an action is performed.\\n * Dialogs: interactive dialogs with 'character' items, in the style of the LucasArts graphic adventures.\\n * Text customization and internationalization.\\n * Custom verbs/commands.\\n * Plugin hooks to customize behavior without modifying the library.\\n\\nI'm waiting for the APIs to stabilize (and get a lot of free time) before fully documenting all those features,\\nbut I'd be happy to write something up if you need help with something specific, just file an issue!\\n\\n## Run on the browser\\n\\nThe codebase is prepared to run both in the terminal with Clojure and the browser with ClojureScript.\\nAn example configuration, using lein-cljsbuild would be:\\n\\n```clojure\\n:cljsbuild\\n {:builds\\n {:main {:source-paths [\\\"src\\\"]\\n :compiler {:output-to \\\"main.js\\\"\\n :main example.core\\n :optimizations :simple\\n :pretty-print false\\n :optimize-constants true\\n :static-fns true}}}\\n```\\n\\nThen the command `lein cljsbuild once` will output a `main.js` file that can be included in any web page to run the game.\\nThe HTML should have a `#terminal` div and include the [jQuery Terminal CSS](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example/blob/master/resources/jquery.terminal-0.11.7.css) to properly render the terminal.\\n\\nThe current limitations of the ClojureScript version of the library are:\\n* No internationalization support (since clojure-gettext does not support ClojureScript).\\n* Can use up to `:simple` optimizations (not `:advanced`), since [ClojureScript self-hosting](https://github.com/clojure/clojurescript/wiki/Optional-Self-hosting) is required for some of the advanced features.\\n\\nSee the [advenjure-example](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure-example) for a game that targets both the terminal and the browser.\\n\\n## Roadmap\\n\\n[Check the milestones](https://github.com/facundoolano/advenjure/milestones).\\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-004\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\".class\":7,\".ctxt\":5,\".java\":5,\"\":1,\".md\":1,\".txt\":1,\".bluej\":1,\".png\":1},\"features\":[\"room\",\"class\",\"item\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"# Adventure Game\\n\\nText based adventure game where, given a map, we were supposed to design a school building wherein the player is supposed to enter a building, find and retrieve a laptop, and exit the building to win. \\n\\nThere are several other objects to collect in the game including a flashlight, candy bar, and more. \\n\\n![Alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zimmertr/Adventure-Game/master/screenshot.png \\\"AG Screenshot\\\")\\n\\n## Winning and Losing\\n\\n**Steps to Win:**\\n\\n1) Move North \\n2) Move West \\n3) Pickup \\n4) Move Up \\n5) Light On \\n6) Move North \\n7) Pickup \\n8) Move South \\n9) Move Down \\n10) Move East \\n11) Move South \\n\\n\\n**Ways to Lose:**\\n\\n1) Break flashlight before collecting laptop - can't collect laptop without it \\n2) Break flashlight while in dark room - die of horror \\n3) Break the laptop any time - the object of the game is to collect the flashlight! \\n\",\"licenseIndicators\":[\"license\"]},{\"id\":\"interactive-fiction-reference-005\",\"sourceGroup\":\"interactive-fiction-reference\",\"fileCounts\":{\"\":2,\".txt\":3,\".java\":6},\"features\":[\"room\",\"item\",\"layer\"],\"readmeExcerpt\":\"Adventure, by Charlie Minges\\n\\n1: Introduction\\n2: Interacting with world\\n3: Goals\\n4: Text file format\\n\\n\\n1: Introduction\\n\\nWelcome to Adventure. In the coming hours, you will embark on a mysterious journey to escape the mysterious\\nlandscape that you have inexplicably woken up in. The best tool you have with you is the power of exploration.\\nIn order to ultimately escape, you will have to explore your surroundings, encountering a variety of items along\\nthe way. \\n\\n2: Interacting with the world\\n\\nNOTE: Commands are NOT case sensitive.\\n\\nLOOK\\nThere are many ways you can interact with the world around you. One of the first things you may want to do is \\nget a better idea of what is around you. To do this, you can use the look command. This will return a description\\nof the room you are in, as well as the possible directions you can move, and any items in the room at the time.\\nTo execute this command, simply type \\\"look\\\" into the console when given the opportunity.\\n\\nLOOK @ OBJECT\\nYou can also look at objects, along with rooms. To look at an object, type \\\"look\\\" followed by the name of the \\nobject you want to look at. It is IMPORTANT TO NOTE that you can only look at objects in your inventory. When \\nthis command is executed, you will be given the name of the object, as well as a short description for it. \\n\\nMOVE\\nThe next thing you will have to do to escape is move. Moving is quite simple. You must be aware that you are \\nallowed to move in the direction you desire from the room you are currently in. This information can be found \\nby looking at the room (SEE LOOK). To move, you either type \\\"move\\\" or \\\"go\\\" into the command line, followed by\\nthe desired direction (in terms of north, south, east, west). You can also just type in the direction you wish \\nto go. If you have moved successfully, a description of the new room you are in will be printed out to the \\nconsole.\\n\\nTAKE\\nItems are an important aspect of Adventure. One way you can interact with them is by taking them. If you are in \\na room that has an item, you can enter \\\"take\\\", or \\\"get\\\", followed by the item name, to add that item to your\\ninventory. This will subsequently remove the object from the rooms inventory.\\n\\nDROP\\nAlong with taking items, you can also drop them. To drop an item from your inventory, simply type in the command\\n\\\"drop\\\", followed by the name of the item you wish to drop. This will add the item to the rooms inventory, and remove\\nit from your own.\\n\\nOTHER\\nThe last two commands available to you, the player, are \\\"inventory\\\" and \\\"score\\\". Inventory will return the names \\nof all the items in your inventory, or tell you if it is empty. Score will return a number representing the score\\nyou have accumulated while playing. They are both accessed by typing in either \\\"inventory\\\" or \\\"score\\\", depending \\non which you want.\\n\\n3: Goals and Scoring\\n\\nThere are a variety of goals that the player should reach throughout the game before being able to escape. A goal \\nwill consist of either taking/dropping an item from/in a particular room, or visiting a particular room. When you \\ncomplete a goal, you get points. You need to complete all goals then visit a particular room in order to escape. The\\ngoal you need to meet for points is 500. Once you have 500 points, you will be directed to a particular particular\\nroom to complete your escape.\\n\\n4: Text file format\\n\\nText files are used to create the rooms and items, as well as guidelines for scoring. Due to this, they need to be\\nset up in a particular way. It is important to note that, whenever using room names, they must match exactly, including\\ncapitalization.\\n\\nROOMS\\nOne room object will read in three different pieces of information: name, neighbors, and description. In the text file,\\nthe information should be organized as follows...\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tname\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tnorth(room name), south(room name), east(room name), west(room name)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tdescription (can extend for multiple lines)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tEND\\nYou must add END, in all caps, at the end of one rooms description, in order for the program to make the distinction \\nthat it is going to make a new room. For the neighbors, put the names of the rooms to the north, south, east, and west\\n(must be done in order shown in example). If there are no neighbors to one direction, use -. You must also include END\\nfor the last rooms text description.\\n\\nITEMS\\nItems are handled in a similar fashion to rooms. They include information regarding name, starting location, and a short\\ndescription. The information should be set up as follows\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tname\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tstarting location (room name)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tdescription (can extend for multiple lines)\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\tEND\\nSimilar to rooms, END must be included at the end, so the program can make the distinction between two objects. You must\\nalso include END after the last items text description.\\n\\nSCORING\\nScoring information includes the type of action (take, drop, visit), the object involved (if there is one), the room it\\nmust take place in, and the points awarded. The information should be set up as follows\\n\\t\\t\\t\\t\\taction, item, room, points\\nIf the action does not involve an item, put a - where an item name would otherwise go. No single segment of information \\nfor one Score object should extend beyond one line.\\n\\n\\nThank you for reading me! MUD codebase written in C#\\n![alt ArchaicQuest II](https://i.imgur.com/LUv3vGm.png)\\n\\n## A MUD codebase to create a multiplayer text based RPG, also known a Multi User Dungeon (MUD)\\n\\nGoal of ArchaicQuest II is to make a MUD that feels nostalgic and compelling to play as well as providing a MUD codebase that makes building and managing your own game simple and fun especially for non coders with the help of the admin tool.\\n\\n[play.archaicquest.com](https://play.archaicquest.com) is the flagship MUD built with ArchaicQuest II.\\n\\n## Current Features\\n- Currently 54 commands, commands can also be abbreviated \ud83d\udd20\\n- Cardinal and Ordinal Movement directions including up and down \ud83e\uddb6\\n- Auto Attack combat rounds \u2694\\n- Skills & spells \ud83d\udcab\\n- 350+ socials \ud83d\ude03 \\n- Look, examine, smell, taste, and touch objects \ud83d\udc41\ud83d\udd0e\ud83d\udc43\ud83d\udc45\ud83e\udd0f\\n- Day and Night cycles \ud83c\udf1e\ud83c\udf1b\\n- Communication among players publicly and privately \ud83d\udcac\\n- NPCs can follow waypoints and execute commands \ud83c\udfad\\n- Ability to add simple or complex quests with Lua Scripting \u2049\\n- Event scripts for NPCs/Rooms for your scripting needs \ud83d\udcdc\\n- Room and NPC emotes \ud83d\udc83\\n\\n## About the Projects\\n\\nArchaicQuest II comprises of [3 projects](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest) that are required together.\\n\\n\\n| Project | Description |\\n| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II) | C# game engine, contains the web API for the admin tool and the SignalR hub for the web socket connects to the client. |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II - Admin tool](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II-Web-Admin) | Angular 8+ web admin, allows creation and management of your MUD world. |\\n| [ArchaicQuest II - Game Client](https://github.com/ArchaicQuest/ArchaicQuest-II-Web-Client) | Angular 8+ web client for connecting to the game and playing with others. |\\n\\n## ArchaicQuest II\\n\\nThe C# project is .NET Core 3.1 and uses [LiteDb](https://www.litedb.org/) which is an embedded NoSQL database. Within Startup.cs it will seed the database on first run with the necessary defaults that are required. \\n\\n* Alignments\\n* AttackTypes\\n* Skills\\n* Races\\n* Status\\n* Classes\\n* Config\\n\\nSome of the above can be edited in the admin tool, the rest if required to be changed needs to be done in code.\\n\\nThe last important step that isn't seeded yet is the very first room! For now before connecting to the game you will need to fire up the web admin tool and create an area and then create a room in said area. Then the web client will be able to connect correctly. \\n\\n### Running the project\\nUse `dotnet run --project ArchaicQuestII.API/ArchaicQuestII.API.csproj`.\\n\\nIf on unix you can use the make file in the project to run using `make run`. \\n\\nFor Windows using visual studio just hit the run button.\\n\\nThere's no output to say it's running but once you make a request it wakes up and responds.\\n\\n### Basic Structure overview\\n\\n- ArchaicQuestII.API\\n - Handles all the API endpoints and initialises everything in Startup.cs\\n- ArchaicQuestII.DataAccess\\n - Wrapper around LiteDB. If not follow the existing structure to add a new interface and class and make sure to update the tests once you add the new interface to Commands.cs \\n\\nTo add new skills and spells use the web admin tool, skills and spells can be scripted with Lua for custom formulas and effects.\\n\\nMajority of features added have been built with the admin tool in mind so most content can be added or modified without coding or making a deployment\\n\\n### Telnet Support\\nTraditionally MUDs use telnet as the way to communicate but with ArchaicQuest II it's web only, the browser can offer a richer, consistent, and streamlined interface for all players without having them to download a client. \\n\\n### Want to get involved?\\nIf you're a coder, writer, MUD player, or someone who wants to help up then get in touch and say 'Hello' on the discord server: [https://discordapp.com/invite/nuf7FVq](https://discordapp.com/invite/nuf7FVq)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Admin Tool\\nView the [ArchaicQuest II - Bilderbeek [1], Rafayel Gardishyan [2], Rob Krueger [2], \\n Rijk van Putten, Joshua van Waardenberg [2]\\n\\n * [1] Corresponding author\\n * [2] Contributed to the work equally, sorted alphabetically on last name \\n\\n## Abstract\\n\\nCity of Thieves is a text adventure in the form of a book.\\nTo beat it, a player has to make the right choices, in a stochastic environment.\\nThe optimal strategy to beat this game is unknown.\\nHere we show the optimal strategy to beat this game.\\n[prime result here].\\n\\n## Introduction\\n\\nIn the 1980's, before the era of computing, adventure books\\nallowed the reader to partake a fictional adventure.\\nAdventure books consisted of hundreds of short chapters in\\na random order. The reader starts at chapter 1 and is asked\\nto do one of multiple actions. Each action takes the player\\nto a next chapter. The player ultimately completes the game\\nor dies.\\n\\n![](Ff5puffin.jpg)\\n\\n> Cover of the first edition of 'City of Thieves'\\n\\nCity of Thieves is a an adventure book written by Ian Livingstone in 1984.\\nThe player should venture to the castle of the protagonist,\\nafter having visited a certain person in a medieval city,\\nthe titular 'City of Thieves'. \\n\\nA character has three statistics: health, skill and luck. \\nMore health allows a player to take more damage,\\nfor example, taking hits in combat.\\nMore skill allows a player to be better in combat,\\nas well as succeed in certain situations, \\nfor example, [example].\\nMore luck allows a player in a situation that requires luck,\\nfor example, when an arrow trap springs, luck may let the player \\navoid the (lethal!) arrow.\\n\\nThese three statistics can be modified within the game.\\nHealth can be increased by certain items, such as food. \\nHealth decreases when taking damage, which is usually in combat,\\nbut can also stem from other physical injuries, such as falling down a wall.\\nSkill can be increased by certain items, such as a better sword.\\nSkill can be decreased by other such items, such as cursed gloves that\\ndecrease the dexterity of the wearer.\\nLuck can be increased by certain events or items, \\nsuch as hearing a blessed song.\\nLuck decreases mostly by using it (see below) or by certain events, such as \\nkilling one of the key characters.\\n\\nThe game starts with a character generation session, \\nsimilar to most RPGs.\\nFor one or more times, 4 dice are rolled.\\nIn a pre-defined order, the dice values determine the\\nplayer's characteristics.\\nA player's skill equals the first dice roll value plus three (this \\ndeviates from the game, see 'Discussion'), the condition is the sum of two dice rolls,\\nwhere luck is the last dice roll value plus six.\\nThe player may roll as often as possible, allowing to get the best values,\\nbut this is quite dull.\\nAccording to Livingstone, the adventure is constructed in such\\na way, that these dice rolls are of less importance. It is unknown,\\nhowever, if the game can be completed with the worst dice rolls.\\n\\nAfter the character generation session, a player may pick\\none of three potions, for either of the three statistics.\\nWhere the health and skill potion refresh their respective value\\nto the initial value, a luck potion does so, as well as add one additional \\npoint. It is an open question, which potion is best to pick\\n\\nAt the start of the game, the player starts with [items] and [number] \\ngold coins. These items may be lost or sold. \\nThe gold coins are used as a currency, to buy items or other situations,\\nsuch as bribing a guard.\\n\\nWithin the actual game, there are multiple kinds of chapters.\\nThe most common type of chapter is to pick one of multiple\\nactions. Sometimes some actions can only be picked after having\\nacquired a certain item [example here].
